NSW.taxYear: Transfer duty: 2026/2027 financial year (contracts dated from 1 July 2026). Land tax: 2026 land tax year (taxing date midnight 31 December 2025, tax charged for calendar 2026).
NSW.landTaxAssessedOn: Unimproved land value (the value of the land itself, excluding buildings or other improvements) as determined annually by the NSW Valuer General as at 1 July each year. Revenue NSW then compares a 3-YEAR AVERAGE of those land values against the threshold (for a parcel created less than 3 years ago, e.g. by subdivision or amalgamation, only the years since creation are averaged). Taxing date is midnight on 31 December each year, and tax is charged for the full following calendar year - liability is NOT pro-rated, so selling mid-year does not reduce it. Land tax AGGREGATES: the threshold is applied to the combined land value of all taxable land the taxpayer owns in NSW, not to each property individually; joint owners get only one threshold for land held together. Site value / capital improved value are not used. Land is taxable unless exempt (principal place of residence, primary production, etc.) - a development site or vacant land held by a company or trust is generally taxable.

landTaxBands.rowText: General threshold: A land value of $1,075,000. NSW.landTaxSurcharges:
SURCHARGE LAND TAX (foreign persons) - 5% of the unimproved land value, for the 2025 land tax year onwards (4% for 2023-2024, 2% for 2018-2022). Source: https://www.revenue.nsw.gov.au/taxes-duties-levies-royalties/land-tax/surcharge-land-tax/what-is-surcharge-land-tax (last updated 8 April 2026). It applies only to RESIDENTIAL land, is payable IN ADDITION to ordinary land tax, has NO tax-free threshold, and applies even if the property is exempt from ordinary land tax. It is assessed per parcel and is proportional to the owner's ownership share, with no joint assessments or secondary deductions. Critically for developers: "residential land" expressly includes vacant land (or land the Chief Commissioner considers mostly vacant) that is zoned or designated for residential or mainly residential use under an environmental planning instrument, as well as land where homes are being built - so a residential development site attracts the 5% surcharge if the owner is foreign. Land used for primary production is excluded. A company is a foreign corporation if a foreign person holds a substantial interest; a trust is foreign if ANY beneficiary (including potential beneficiaries of a discretionary trust) is a foreign person, and a discretionary trust deed must IRREVOCABLY exclude foreign beneficiaries (both a "no foreign beneficiary requirement" and a "no amendment requirement") to escape the surcharge. Exemptions/concessions/refunds may be available to Australian-based developers that own and develop residential land, and for build-to-rent projects.

TRUST TREATMENT (not a surcharge, but it removes the threshold - highly relevant to trust-held development sites). Source: https://www.revenue.nsw.gov.au/taxes-duties-levies-royalties/land-tax/understanding-land-tax/types-of-landowners/trusts (last updated 22 July 2026). A SPECIAL TRUST - which includes family trusts, discretionary trusts, unit trusts that do not satisfy the fixed-trust criteria in s 3A(3B) Land Tax Management Act 1956, and trusts created by a will - receives NO land tax threshold and is instead "taxed at a flat rate of 1.6% for amounts up to the premium land tax threshold, then at 2%". Revenue NSW's own example: a family trust owning land valued $600,000 pays $600,000 x 1.6% = $9,600 despite being far below the $1,075,000 general threshold, with a 2% premium marginal rate above $6,571,000. Fixed trusts, bare trusts, complying superannuation trusts, concessional trusts, and some family unit trusts DO receive the threshold. Related companies may also be denied a separate threshold.

NO ABSENTEE-OWNER SURCHARGE and NO VACANT RESIDENTIAL LAND TAX equivalent (the Victorian-style measures) were found on Revenue NSW for the 2026 land tax year - see "unresolved".

PREMIUM DUTY IS NOT INCLUDED IN dutyBands and must be implemented separately. 2026/2027: dutiable value over $3,870,000 -> $194,137 plus $7.00 for every $100 over $3,870,000 (rate 0.07). Premium duty applies ONLY to RESIDENTIAL land, so it must NOT be applied to a commercial, industrial or non-residential-zoned development site. Where a property above the threshold is part business, only the residential portion is subject to the premium rate; for parcels over 2 hectares the premium rate applies only to the first 2 hectares as a proportion of overall value, with the remainder at the general rate. dutyBands as transcribed is the pure general/section-32 scale with an open-ended top band, which is the correct schedule for a developer buying a non-residential site.

$100 ROUNDING NOT CONFIRMED FOR THE GENERAL SCALE. The premium property duty guide says the rate is charged for every $100 'or part' of the excess, and the Duties Act 1997 s 32 scale is expressed the same way, but the current general rate table on the calculate page does not state 'or part thereof'. I could not confirm from a primary source whether Revenue NSW rounds the dutiable value up to the next whole $100 before applying the marginal rate. The effect is at most a few dollars, but a byte-exact match against Revenue NSW's online calculator may need this.

FIRST DUTY BAND kind: recorded as 'flat' (fixed 0, rate 0.0125) because the source wording is bare - '$1.25 for every $100 (minimum $20)' - with no fixed component and no 'over $X'. Because this band starts at $0, flat and marginal are arithmetically IDENTICAL here (0 + (value - 0) x 0.0125 = value x 0.0125), so this classification cannot cause a mispricing either way. Bands 2-6 are unambiguously marginal ('plus $X for every $100 over $Y'). I found NO flat band anywhere in the NSW general duty scale - unlike Victoria's $960,000-$2,000,000 band, no NSW band applies a rate to the whole dutiable value.

SURCHARGE PURCHASER DUTY (a DUTY surcharge, not captured by any field in this schema) - currently a flat 9% of the dutiable value, paid IN ADDITION to transfer duty, where a foreign person acquires residential-related property in NSW. The current page states 9%; the past-rates page lists only '1 July 2017 - 31 December 2024: 8%' and '21 June 2016 - 30 June 2017: 4%', so the 9% rate applies from 1 January 2025. Revenue NSW notes this rate is NOT CPI-indexed. A foreign-owned developer buying a residential-zoned site would face 9% on top of the general duty above; this is a very large number on a multi-million-dollar site and must be handled explicitly in the feasibility model.

LANDHOLDER DUTY not transcribed: acquiring a significant interest in a company or unit trust with NSW landholdings over $2 million can trigger landholder duty instead of / in addition to transfer duty. Relevant if the site is acquired via an entity purchase rather than a land transfer. I did not open that page, so its rates and the 'significant interest' percentages are unverified here.

NO NSW EQUIVALENT of Victoria's absentee-owner surcharge or vacant residential land tax was found on any Revenue NSW page I read. I did not exhaustively search for one, so treat this as 'not found' rather than 'confirmed absent'. NSW does have surcharge land tax (foreign persons) as described.

NO LAND TAX EXEMPTION FOR LAND UNDER DEVELOPMENT was confirmed. The exemptions pages list principal place of residence, primary production, boarding houses, aged care, childcare, caravan parks and non-profits; I did not open the full 'other exemptions' page, so I cannot confirm or rule out a build-to-rent or developer concession for ORDINARY land tax (the developer/build-to-rent concessions I did confirm relate to SURCHARGE land tax). A holding-cost model should assume a development site held by a company or trust is fully liable for ordinary land tax each year until sold, and verify any concession independently.

LAND TAX THRESHOLDS ARE FROZEN, DUTY THRESHOLDS ARE NOT. The 2024-25 State Budget froze the general ($1,075,000) and premium ($6,571,000) land tax thresholds for all land tax years after 2024, so these figures are stable for multi-year cash-flow modelling. By contrast the transfer duty and premium duty thresholds and fixed amounts are re-indexed to CPI EVERY 1 JULY, so the duty bands above will change on 1 July 2027 and must be re-scraped annually. The applicable duty rate year is set by the CONTRACT DATE (or the date of transfer if there is no contract), not the settlement date.

VIC.landTaxAssessedOn: Site value, as determined by the Valuer-General Victoria, of all taxable land the owner held as at midnight on 31 December of the year preceding the year of assessment (i.e. 31 December 2025 for the 2026 land tax year). Land tax applies for a calendar year. It is assessed on the TOTAL taxable value of all the taxpayer's Victorian land holdings aggregated together (grouping rules apply to related corporations), not property by property, so a developer's new site pushes the whole portfolio up the scale. Land used as the owner's principal place of residence is exempt; these are the general (non-PPR) rates that apply to development sites, vacant land and investment holdings.
VIC.landTaxSurcharges:
TRUST SURCHARGE: land held on trust is assessed on a separate, harsher schedule from the 2024 land tax year with a lower $25,000 threshold - $25,000 to <$50,000: $82 plus 0.375% of amount >$25,000; $50,000 to <$100,000: $676 plus 0.375%; $100,000 to <$250,000: $1338 plus 0.375%; $250,000 to <$600,000: $1901 plus 0.675%; $600,000 to <$1,000,000: $4263 plus 0.975%; $1,000,000 to <$1,800,000: $8163 plus 1.275%; $1,800,000 to <$3,000,000: $18,363 plus 1.1072%; $3,000,000 and over: $31,650 plus 2.65% (the trust surcharge phases out at $3m, where it converges with the general rate). Directly relevant here: a developer buying through a trust is on this schedule, not the general one. The SRO publishes a separate land tax trust calculator.

ABSENTEE OWNER SURCHARGE (AOS): 4% from the 2024 land tax year (2% for 2020-2023), applied on top of the general and trust surcharge rates. Applies to an absentee individual, absentee corporation or trustee of an absentee trust who is an absentee owner at 31 December. It does not apply to Australian citizens or permanent residents living overseas. From 1 January 2026 New Zealand citizens are subject to the same rules as other foreign citizens. Not payable where the land is exempt, where total taxable value is below $50,000, or where trust-held land is below $25,000 and the trust surcharge rate applies. The published general-with-AOS schedule runs: $50,000 to <$100,000 $2500 plus 4%; $100,000 to <$300,000 $4975 plus 4%; $300,000 to <$600,000 $13,350 plus 4.3%; $600,000 to <$1,000,000 $26,250 plus 4.6%; $1,000,000 to <$1,800,000 $44,650 plus 4.9%; $1,800,000 to <$3,000,000 $83,850 plus 5.65%; $3,000,000 and over $151,650 plus 6.65%. Exemptions may be available to Australian-incorporated absentee corporations running a commercial operation in Victoria using local labour, materials and services, and to some build-to-rent developments (the BTR exemption ends once the development is complete and the owner becomes a passive investor).

VACANT RESIDENTIAL LAND TAX (VRLT): a separate tax from land tax, assessed on CAPITAL IMPROVED VALUE rather than site value, with no threshold. Escalating: 1% of CIV in the first year the land is liable, 2% in the second consecutive year, 3% in the third or later consecutive year (before 2025 it was a flat 1%). Two cases are pegged at 1% of CIV regardless: (a) land in metropolitan Melbourne that has remained undeveloped for a continuous period of 5 years or more and is capable of residential development, and (b) new residential land unused, unoccupied and unsold for more than 3 years. Both limbs bite directly on a developer landbanking a metro site or holding unsold completed stock.

FOREIGN PURCHASER ADDITIONAL DUTY (duty side, not land tax): 8% of the dutiable value for contracts, transactions, agreements and arrangements entered into on or after 1 July 2019 (7% from 1 July 2016; 3% from 1 July 2015), charged on top of the general duty above where a foreign purchaser acquires residential property.

No minimum duty amount is published on the SRO rates page. dutyMinimum is set to 0 on that basis rather than on a positive SRO statement - Victoria's bottom band is a straight 1.4% with no stated floor. Rounding conventions are likewise not published on the rate pages.

BOUNDARY CONVENTION MISMATCH between the two schedules, and it is not cosmetic. Duty bands are written inclusive-of-upper with the next band opening at '>' the same figure ('>$130,000 - $960,000'), so $960,000 exactly sits in the 6% marginal band. Land tax bands are written 'X to < Y', so upTo is EXCLUSIVE - $300,000 exactly falls in the $300,000-to-<$600,000 row, not the row below. Implement land tax lookups as from <= value < upTo.

The first three land tax rows are FIXED DOLLAR AMOUNTS with no marginal component ($500 for $50,000-<$100,000, $975 for $100,000-<$300,000), not rates. I encoded them as fixed with rate 0, which reproduces them exactly under the marginal formula, but the schedule is genuinely discontinuous: $299,999 of holdings attracts $975 while $300,000 attracts $1350. That step is in the SRO source, not a transcription artefact.

The duty schedule is also genuinely discontinuous at $960,000 because of the flat band: $960,000 attracts $2870 + 6% x $830,000 = $52,670, but $960,001 attracts 5.5% of the WHOLE value = $52,800. Check that no implementation smooths this over. The flat character of the $960,000-$2,000,000 band is confirmed by the source wording '5.5% of the dutiable value' with no 'in excess of' clause, in both the HTML table and the SRO CSV.

COMMERCIAL / INDUSTRIAL SITES MAY NOT BE ON THIS DUTY SCHEDULE AT ALL. Under the Commercial and Industrial Property Tax Reform Act 2024, from 1 July 2024 commercial and industrial property in Victoria pays land transfer (stamp) duty one final time on an eligible dutiable transaction and then enters the CIPT reform, after which later dealings can be exempt from land transfer and landholder duty and an annual CIPT on land value becomes payable 10 years after entry. The SRO landing page confirms that mechanism but does NOT state the CIPT rate, and I found no SRO 'current rates' page for CIPT - so the commonly cited 1% figure is UNVERIFIED from a primary source here. For a developer buying a commercial or industrial site this materially changes both the acquisition duty and the holding-cost model. Required follow-up.

Which regime applies turns on the site's actual and intended qualifying use (residential vs commercial/industrial per the AVPCC) and on whether the vendor's property has already entered the CIPT reform. Transaction-specific; not resolvable from rate pages.

Landholder duty (acquiring an interest in a land-rich entity rather than the land itself) and the Part 4A sub-sale / land development provisions of the Duties Act 2000 are NOT modelled in these bands. Both are common in development deals - a nomination after land development work has begun can trigger duty twice. The SRO premium duty page confirms that where a nomination is a Part 4A sub-sale trigger event (additional consideration or land development), the subsequent transaction is treated as entered into on the nomination date.

The premium rate does not apply to a dutiable transaction occurring on or after 1 July 2021 that was made pursuant to an agreement or arrangement entered into BEFORE 1 July 2021 - including a paid written option to purchase or a sufficiently certain Heads of Agreement. Historical rates then apply (flat 5.5% above $960,000, no $2m premium band). Only the current schedule is encoded here.

I did not independently confirm that no rate change after 20 July 2026 is pending. The pages carry SRO 'Updated' dates of 10 July 2026 (duty) and 20 July 2026 (land tax), and the land tax page states the rates run for the 2024-2033 land tax years, but a later State Taxation Acts amendment would not be reflected. Re-scrape both pages before relying on them for a live acquisition.

QLD.landTaxAssessedOn: Total taxable value of all freehold land the owner holds in Queensland at midnight 30 June (for the 2026-27 year, midnight 30 June 2026). Land tax AGGREGATES across the taxpayer's holdings: all land owned solely plus the owner's share (interest) in land owned jointly with others. Each entity is assessed separately, so land held by a company, by an individual, and by that person as trustee are three separate aggregations with separate assessment notices. Per QRO, the 'taxable value' of each parcel for a financial year is the LESSER of (a) the Land Valuation Act 2010 value (the statutory land value determined by the Valuer-General at 30 June, issued in the annual land valuation notice) and (b) the averaged value — the average of the statutory land value for the current and previous 2 financial years, or, where the previous 2 years are unavailable, the current year's statutory land value multiplied by that year's averaging factor (0.90 for 30 June 2025, 0.89 for 2024, 0.88 for 2023, 0.87 for 2022, 0.98 for 2021, 0.96 for 2020). Parcel taxable values are determined separately then summed. So land tax is NOT simply the current site value — for rising valuations the 3-year averaging usually gives a lower base. Exemptions (e.g. home, primary production) remove that land's taxable value from the aggregate.

landTaxBands.rowText: $10,000,000 or more | $187,500 plus 2.75 cents for each $1 more than $10,000,000

QLD.landTaxSurcharges: FOREIGN COMPANY / FOREIGN TRUST SURCHARGE (land tax): a foreign company (incorporated outside Australia, or in which foreign persons or related persons hold a controlling interest of at least 50%) or a trustee of a foreign trust pays a 3% surcharge on taxable land valued at $350,000 or more, IN ADDITION to the land tax rates above. QRO's own worked wording for the equivalent absentee surcharge computes it as (taxable value − $350,000) × 3%, i.e. only the excess above $350,000 is surcharged, not the whole value. The foreign company/trust rate table itself (https://qro.qld.gov.au/land-tax/calculate/foreign-company-trust/) is identical to the company/trust table transcribed above ($1,450 + 1.7c; $33,750 + 1.5c; $75,000 + 2.25c; $187,500 + 2.75c), so for a foreign corporate developer only the 3% surcharge is added. ABSENTEE SURCHARGE (individuals only, not relevant to a company/trust developer): an absentee — a foreign individual who does not hold a permanent visa and does not usually live in Australia — pays a 3% surcharge on taxable land valued at $350,000 or more, calculated as (taxable value − $350,000) × 3%, and is assessed on a DIFFERENT rate table whose top two bands are lower than the corporate table: $5,000,000–$9,999,999 = $75,000 plus 2.0 cents per $1 over $5,000,000, and $10,000,000 or more = $175,000 plus 2.5 cents per $1 over $10,000,000. Absentees cannot claim the home or primary production exemption. TRUSTS: no surcharge, but structural rules matter. Trust land is registered in the trustee's name and each trust is assessed separately, as if that trust's Queensland land were the only land the trustee owned; land held for a trust is NOT added to land the same person holds as an individual, as a company, or as trustee of another trust — unless it is a cloned trust. TRUST AGGREGATION applies where, at 30 June, a taxpayer is trustee of more than one trust and the beneficiaries of those trusts and their interests are the same: the trusts' landholdings are then combined into one assessment. Land held by 2 or more trustees of the same trust is assessed as if owned by 1 person. SPECIAL DISABILITY TRUST: from 30 June 2022 the trustee is treated as an individual — $600,000 threshold and the individual rate table. NO VACANT LAND SURCHARGE: Queensland publishes no land tax vacant-land or under-utilised-land surcharge (unlike some other states); a held development site is taxed on the ordinary schedule. A build-to-rent concession (a reduction, not a surcharge) exists at https://qro.qld.gov.au/land-tax/relief/build-to-rent/ and was not transcribed. SEPARATELY, ON THE DUTY SIDE (not land tax): additional foreign acquirer duty (AFAD) of 8% applies on top of transfer duty, landholder duty and corporate trustee duty for acquisitions of AFAD RESIDENTIAL land by foreign persons including companies and trusts.
unresolved: ROUNDING RULE NOT MODELLED BY A PLAIN LINEAR FORMULA: every QLD duty band says '$X for each $100, OR PART OF $100, over $Y'. The marginal step is therefore charged on the excess ROUNDED UP to the next whole $100, i.e. duty = fixed + ceil((value - from)/100) x rate x 100, not fixed + (value - from) x rate. For round-numbered site prices the two agree exactly; for an odd value (e.g. $1,234,567) the linear formula understates duty by up to one $100 step (max $5.75). Our band shape stores the plain rate — implement the ceiling if cent-exact assessment matching is required.

dutyMinimum RECORDED AS 0 BECAUSE NO MINIMUM DUTY IS PUBLISHED ON THE RATES PAGE. The rates page states only 'Not more than $5,000 | Nil'. The separate 'How to calculate' page adds that 'no duty is payable on the transfer of property valued at less than $5,000' but such transfers must still be assessed and stamped. A distinct $5 duty applies to transfers of a mortgage solely over Queensland land (mortgage duty itself was abolished 1 July 2008) — that is a separate head, not a minimum on land transfers. I could not confirm any general minimum duty amount from a QRO primary source.

dutyPremiumThreshold RECORDED AS 0: Queensland publishes no premium / luxury duty threshold. The top band simply runs from $1,000,000 upward at $5.75 per $100. The only value-linked add-on is the 8% AFAD for foreign acquirers of residential land, which is a surcharge on the whole dutiable value rather than a premium band.

BAND BOUNDARY WORDING IS AMBIGUOUS AT THE SEAMS. QRO writes 'More than $5,000 up to $75,000', then '$75,000 to $540,000', then '$540,000 to $1,000,000', then 'More than $1,000,000' — so $75,000, $540,000 and $1,000,000 each appear in two adjacent rows. This is harmless because the schedule is arithmetically continuous at every seam (I checked: 1.5% x $70,000 = $1,050; $1,050 + 3.5% x $465,000 = $17,325; $17,325 + 4.5% x $460,000 = $38,025), so either reading gives the same duty. Our band boundaries use half-open [from, upTo) intervals.

ALL FIVE DUTY BANDS CLASSIFIED AS MARGINAL, with confidence. Every non-nil row is worded 'plus $X for each $100 over $Y', with an explicit fixed amount for the value below the threshold, and QRO's own worked example decomposes it that way ('$17,325 for the first $540,000' + '$4.50 for every $100 in $310,000, the balance above $540,000'). There is no flat / whole-of-value band in the Queensland general schedule, unlike Victoria's $960,000-$2,000,000 band.

LAND TAX SCHEDULE CHOSEN: companies and trusts (non-foreign). The brief's developer is a company or trust, so this is the correct table and its $350,000 threshold applies. NOTE that Queensland does not vary the RATE by principal-place-of-residence status the way some states do — there is no separate 'general/investment' land tax table. Instead a single table per owner type applies and the owner's home is removed via a home EXEMPTION. For a corporate developer holding a development site no home exemption is available, so the full table applies. If the acquiring entity is instead an individual, a different table and a $600,000 threshold apply (https://qro.qld.gov.au/land-tax/calculate/individual/): $600,000-$999,999 = $500 + 1.0c per $1 over $600,000; $1,000,000-$2,999,999 = $4,500 + 1.65c; $3,000,000-$4,999,999 = $37,500 + 1.25c; $5,000,000-$9,999,999 = $62,500 + 1.75c; $10,000,000+ = $150,000 + 2.25c.

SITE VALUE vs UNIMPROVED VALUE NOT CONFIRMED FROM QRO. The QRO taxable-value page says only 'Land Valuation Act 2010 value (statutory land value) of the land on 30 June' and links out to qld.gov.au for the valuation methodology. The Land Valuation Act 2010 distinction (site value for non-rural land, unimproved value for rural land) is therefore NOT sourced from qro.qld.gov.au and I have deliberately not asserted it in landTaxAssessedOn. For a specific site, take the basis stated on that property's annual land valuation notice.

AVERAGING FACTOR FOR 30 JUNE 2026 NOT PUBLISHED AS AT SCRAPE. The QRO averaging-factor table (last updated 24 July 2025) runs only to 30 June 2025 (0.90). The 2026-27 factor, needed to value a parcel with fewer than 3 years of statutory values (e.g. a freshly subdivided development lot), was not available from a primary source. Re-check https://qro.qld.gov.au/land-tax/about/taxable-value/ before relying on averaged values for a 30 June 2026 liability.

SA.landTaxAssessedOn: Site value (the Valuer-General's site value of the land, i.e. land value excluding improvements — explicitly NOT capital value), assessed on ownership and property details as at midnight on 30 June immediately preceding the financial year (so 30 June 2026 for the 2026-27 year). Land tax aggregates: where an ownership holds more than one taxable property, all taxable site values are added together (aggregated) to give the "total taxable site value" for that ownership, the rate scale is applied to that aggregate, and the resulting tax is then apportioned back to each taxable property in proportion to its site value. Exempt land (e.g. the owner's principal place of residence) is excluded from the aggregate and has no tax apportioned to it. Each ownership (individual, joint, trust, corporate group) is assessed separately; land held in a joint ownership is assessed first in the joint ownership and again in each owner's individual ownership at their share, with a deduction applied to prevent double taxation. All members of a corporate group are assessed as if a single owner at the general rates. Owners are jointly and severally liable. De minimis: if the aggregate exceeds the threshold but calculated land tax is less than $20, no Land Tax Assessment is issued. Thresholds are indexed annually by the Valuer-General's average site value change (2026-27 index value 2.08, average percentage change 12.44%) and gazetted by 30 June; rates themselves were unchanged for 2026-27.

SA.landTaxSurcharges: SA has NO absentee, foreign-owner or vacant-residential-land LAND TAX surcharge. There is no land tax surcharge schedule at all — instead SA operates a second, separate rate scale for land held on trust. TRUST LAND TAX RATES (2026-27, a distinct scale — do not fold into the general bands): threshold only $25,000; exceeds $25,000 but not $936,000 = $125 plus $0.50 per $100 above $25,000; exceeds $936,000 but not $1,504,000 = $4,680 plus $1.00 per $100 above $936,000; exceeds $1,504,000 but not $2,188,000 = $10,360 plus $1.50 per $100 above $1,504,000; exceeds $2,188,000 but not $3,504,000 = $20,620 plus $2.40 per $100 above $2,188,000; exceeds $3,504,000 = $52,204 plus $2.40 per $100 above $3,504,000. This matters directly to a developer buying through a trust: land acquired by a DISCRETIONARY trust after midnight 16 October 2019 is always assessed at trust rates, with no exception, so a site bought in a discretionary trust attracts the $25,000 threshold and the surcharged trust scale rather than the $936,000 general threshold. A fixed or unit trust is assessed at the GENERAL rates only if the trustee has notified RevenueSA of ALL beneficiaries or unitholders (partial nominations are not permitted); otherwise trust rates apply. Excluded trusts, and a corporate trustee that is part of a corporate group and does not hold the land on trust, are assessed at general rates. Trustees must notify RevenueSA within one month of acquiring land on trust or interest and penalty tax may apply. Each trust ownership is assessed separately and is not aggregated with other trusts or with the trustee's own land. SEPARATE STAMP DUTY SURCHARGE (not land tax): a Foreign Purchaser acquiring RESIDENTIAL land in SA pays a foreign ownership surcharge of 7% of the value of the interest acquired in the residential land, in addition to any conveyance duty, applying from 1 January 2018; it is calculated on the GST-inclusive amount and pro-rated to the fractional interest acquired (7% of $600,000 = $42,000). A corporation that becomes a foreign corporation within 3 years after acquisition can be caught retrospectively. Ex-gratia relief guidelines exist for significant developments.
unresolved: CRITICAL FOR A DEVELOPER — SA may charge NO conveyance duty at all on the site being acquired. Since 1 July 2018 no liability to duty arises on a conveyance or transfer of an interest in non-residential and non-primary-production land ('qualifying land'). The transcribed duty scale therefore only applies to RESIDENTIAL and PRIMARY PRODUCTION land. Qualifying land (duty-free) covers Land Use Codes: Commercial 2000-2999, Industrial 3100-3999, Vacant Land 4110-4600 (with exceptions), Institutions 5100-5990, Public Utilities 6100-6990, Recreation 7100-7900, Mining and Quarrying 8100-8409, plus Hotel 1810, Motel 1820, Hotel/Motel Community 1831. Still DUTIABLE: Residential 1100-1999, Primary Production 9100-9994, Vacant Land Urban 4100, Vacant Land with minor improvements Urban 4101, Vacant Land rural residential 4150, Vacant Land with minor improvements Rural Living 4151. So a vacant urban development site in a residential zone IS dutiable, while a vacant site in a commercial/industrial zone is NOT. The determinant is the Valuer-General's land use code plus zoning under the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act 2016 — the tool cannot infer this from purchase price alone and should ask the user, or it will materially overstate acquisition cost on commercial/industrial sites.

A naive `fixed + (value - from) * rate` will understate duty by up to $5.49 and land tax by up to $2.39. Verified wording present in all rows of both tables.

I could not confirm from a primary source whether the Stamp Duties Act 1923 imposes a separate statutory minimum.

Duty is charged on the greater of the land value (including improvements) or the consideration including GST — not simply the contract price. WA.landTaxAssessedOn: Unimproved value of the land as determined by the Valuer-General (NOT site value, and not capital/improved value). Per RevenueWA: "The taxable value for land is the lesser of the current unimproved value of the land or 150% of the previous year's unimproved value" — a per-parcel cap applied before aggregation. Assessment date: ownership at midnight on 30 June immediately preceding the assessment (financial) year — i.e. 30 June 2026 for the 2026-27 assessment year. Land tax AGGREGATES across a taxpayer's holdings: "Land tax is calculated on the aggregated taxable value of all non-exempt land held in the same ownership at midnight on 30 June" — if you own more than one lot the valuations are added together before tax is calculated, then a single rate is applied to the aggregate. Aggregation is strictly by identical ownership capacity: land owned solely by you is not combined with land you own jointly with another person, nor with land you hold an interest in through a company or trust; those are assessed separately. Liability attaches to land NOT used as the owner's principal place of residence (so a developer's site or vacant land held for development is assessable). A vendor who sells between 1 July and 30 June remains liable on the basis of ownership at the preceding 30 June. A newly subdivided lot becomes assessable from the 30 June following approval of the subdivision, even if no certificate of title has issued. Notices of assessment generally issue between September and January.
WA.landTaxSurcharges:
METROPOLITAN REGION IMPROVEMENT TAX (MRIT) — this is the one real add-on in WA and it is levied IN ADDITION TO land tax on property in the Perth metropolitan area, to finance land for roads, open space and parks. Verbatim rate rows from the same RevenueWA page: "$0 - $300,000 | Nil" and "$300,001 + | 0.0014 dollars for each $1 in excess of $300,000". So MRIT is a flat 0.14% marginal charge above the same $300,000 threshold, with no upper cap and no bracket structure. For metro land, model total annual liability as land tax (from landTaxBands) PLUS MRIT. Whether the land falls in the metropolitan region is determined by the LGA map RevenueWA publishes (Metropolitan_Perth_LGA_boundaries.pdf). MRIT is deliberately kept out of landTaxBands.

NO FOREIGN / ABSENTEE / VACANT-LAND LAND TAX SURCHARGE. RevenueWA publishes no absentee-owner or foreign-owner land tax surcharge, no separate higher trust/company land tax rate, and no vacant residential land tax equivalent to Victoria's. A developer land-banking a WA site pays the ordinary general rates above plus MRIT if metro. (See "unresolved" — this is inferred from the absence of any such page rather than an explicit denial by RevenueWA.)

TRUSTS — differently assessed, not surcharged. A trustee "will be liable for any land tax assessed on land you hold as a trustee as if the land was your own unless you hold the land in trust for different persons." Where land is held in trust for different persons, land tax is assessed separately on the land held for each separate trust. Land held as trustee is assessed separately from land the same person owns beneficially (though in certain circumstances it will be assessed jointly). Land used as a trustee's principal place of residence is NOT exempt unless specifically held for a disabled beneficiary who resides there. Trust ownership must be advised to RevenueWA in writing with the endorsed Offer and Acceptance and the Deed of Trust.

JOINT OWNERSHIP. Jointly held land is assessed separately from land owned solely and from land held with any other combination of owners — each distinct ownership combination is its own aggregation set. This can be used to keep aggregates below thresholds, but only where ownership genuinely differs.

LEASES FROM GOVERNMENT. A lessee of land from the WA Government, a government agency, local government or public statutory authority is treated as the owner and is liable for land tax; a rebate may apply if such a lease is involuntarily terminated before expiry.

DUTY-SIDE SURCHARGE (not land tax, recorded here because there is no other field for it). Foreign transfer duty of 7% of the dutiable value applies to a foreign person acquiring residential property, and RevenueWA's definition of residential property expressly captures development sites: "land which a person intends to develop into residential properties or subdivide to enable another person to construct a home or apartment on the land" and "land on which a person intends to construct a residence". A foreign corporation includes any corporation incorporated outside Australia or in which foreign persons control at least 50% of voting power or hold at least 50% of issued shares; a foreign trustee is the trustee of a foreign trust. This 7% is charged on top of the general-rate duty, is assessed at purchase, and may be reassessed and refunded if the development produces ten or more residential dwellings or lots on which ten or more dwellings can be constructed (Form FDA43). Legislation (Finance Legislation Amendment (Housing Affordability) Bill 2026) was before Parliament as at 18 June 2026 to add a "build-to-sell" exemption and amend the existing foreign developer exemptions — not yet law.

Taxable value per parcel is the lesser of current unimproved value or 150% of the prior year's unimproved value. A feasibility model that feeds a raw current UV straight into landTaxBands will overstate land tax in a year of sharp valuation growth. Implementing this requires the prior year's UV, which the tool may not hold.

TAS.landTaxAssessedOn: Assessed land value (unimproved land value, not site/capital value) as shown on the land tax assessment notice. The Office of the Valuer-General determines assessed land value annually on 1 July; where a council district is not revalued that year, market-based adjustment factors are applied to existing land values. Liability is set by ownership and land classification as at 1 July each year (the assessment date). Where an owner holds more than one taxable property, the assessed land value of each property is aggregated (added together) within each land classification and land tax is calculated on the total aggregated value - so a developer's whole general-land portfolio is taxed on one combined value, not property by property.
TAS.landTaxSurcharges: Foreign Investor Land Tax Surcharge (FILTS): 2 per cent of the assessed land value of the foreign-owned portion of land classified as General Land, where the land was acquired by a foreign person on or after 1 July 2022, or is owned by a company or trust that became foreign on or after 1 July 2022, AND the land may be, or is capable of, being lawfully used solely or primarily for residential purposes. Land acquired by a foreign person before 1 July 2022 is not subject to FILTS unless a further interest is acquired on or after that date. FILTS can be payable even where the assessed land value is below the land tax threshold, so a foreign-owned residential development site can attract FILTS with nil ordinary land tax. Source: https://www.sro.tas.gov.au/land-tax/foreign-investor-land-tax-surcharge/rate-of-surcharge. Aggregation/grouping (not a rate surcharge but it raises the effective rate): related companies - those with a common controlling interest or that are related bodies corporate under the Corporations Act 2001 - have their land values aggregated and are assessed on the aggregate; a trustee's landholdings are aggregated unless the trustee is a registered trustee company, an executor/administrator/guardian/committee/receiver/liquidator, the Public Trustee, or a court-appointed trustee. Land held by a taxpayer as trustee is NOT aggregated with land that taxpayer holds in their own right. Tasmania has no separate trust surcharge rate, no absentee-owner land tax surcharge, and no vacant-land land tax surcharge (vacant land is simply General Land, taxable at the general scale). Sources: https://www.sro.tas.gov.au/Documents/land-tax-guideline.pdf and https://www.sro.tas.gov.au/land-tax/rates-of-land-tax.

ACT.landTaxAssessedOn: Average Unimproved Value (AUV) of the parcel - the average of the property's unimproved value over up to 5 years. For 2026-27 the AUV is the average of the property's unimproved value as at 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026. Land tax has TWO components and the bands below are only the second: (1) a FIXED CHARGE of $1,778 per year from 1 July 2026, plus (2) a valuation charge from the marginal AUV bands. The tool must add the fixed charge to the banded amount. Assessed QUARTERLY on the status of the property at four key dates - 1 July, 1 October, 1 January and 1 April each year - for each whole quarter, with no daily pro-rata within a quarter; the annual figure is split 25.2054% (Jul-Sep), 25.2054% (Oct-Dec), 24.6575% (Jan-Mar), 24.9315% (Apr-Jun) in a non-leap year (25.1366 / 25.1366 / 24.8633 / 24.8633 in a leap year). Scope: applies to ACT RESIDENTIAL land that is not the owner's principal place of residence, including rented property, VACANT property, property owned as trustee, and rented secondary dwellings (granny flats, apportioned by rented floor area). Land tax does NOT apply to commercial property at all. Each property is assessed SEPARATELY - see unresolved re: no aggregation. Unit-title residential properties multiply the complex's valuation charge by the unit entitlement percentage.

ACT.landTaxSurcharges: FOREIGN OWNERSHIP SURCHARGE: a foreign person who owns residential land in the ACT pays a land tax surcharge of 0.75 per cent of the Average Unimproved Value per year (applying from 1 July 2018 onwards). It is charged in addition to any land tax payable because the property is not a principal place of residence, and is calculated as part of the land tax assessment. A "foreign person" is a foreign individual (not an Australian citizen, permanent resident, NZ citizen holding a Special Category Visa, or a person ordinarily resident in Australia), a foreign corporation (incorporated outside Australia, or in which one or more foreign persons hold a controlling interest of 50 per cent or more of shares or voting power), or the trustee of a foreign trust (foreign persons and their associates holding 50 per cent or more of the beneficial interests; for a discretionary trust only where the foreign person is specifically named in the deed as a possible distributee). Liability is tested on the first day of each land tax quarter, beginning the first quarter after settlement. Notification to the Commissioner is required and penalties apply for failure to notify. Where foreign-owned land is occupied under a nil or nominal rent arrangement, the owner is liable for the surcharge but exempt from land tax itself. Relevant guidance: Revenue Circular LTA002 Foreign Ownership Surcharge. TRUSTS: property owned as trustee is expressly liable for ordinary land tax, but the ACT publishes NO separate trust surcharge rate or lower trust threshold (unlike NSW/Vic). ABSENTEE: no absentee-owner surcharge is published; an owner posted overseas is not treated as a foreign owner (though land tax may apply on a long-term posting). VACANT LAND / VACANT RESIDENTIAL: no separate vacant-land or vacancy surcharge rate - vacant residential property is simply liable for ordinary land tax at the rates above. No commercial or industrial land tax exists in the ACT, so no surcharge arises on a commercial site.

ACT LAND TAX DOES NOT AGGREGATE ACROSS A TAXPAYER'S HOLDINGS - contrary to the assumption in the task brief. Each liable property is assessed separately on its own AUV, with its own fixed charge, and the marginal bands restart for each parcel. The revenue office pages describe assessment per property (including the unit-entitlement apportionment for unit titles) and nowhere describe aggregation of a taxpayer's total landholdings. There is no 'landholdings aggregation' or 'joint ownership assessment' page on the site equivalent to the NSW/Vic ones. I could not find any primary-source statement that either confirms or denies aggregation in so many words, so treat 'no aggregation' as a strong inference rather than a quoted rule.

NO LAND TAX ON COMMERCIAL PROPERTY. 'Land tax does not apply to commercial properties' (About land tax page). So a site the developer declares as commercial attracts no ACT land tax holding cost at all - a material feasibility input that the band table alone will not tell you.

dutyBands.rowText: WARNING - THIS BAND IS A QUADRATIC FORMULA AND CANNOT BE EXPRESSED AS fixed + rate. DO NOT USE fixed/rate ABOVE (deliberately set to 0 so a naive implementation fails loudly rather than producing a plausible wrong number). Verbatim TRO wording (I-SD-002 / I-GEN-001): 'Where the dutiable value is less than $525 000, duty is calculated with the following formula: D = (0.06571441 x V2) + 15V  where D = the duty payable in $ and V = the dutiable value / 1000'. Implement as: V = value / 1000; duty = 0.06571441 * V * V + 15 * V. Equivalently duty = 0.06571441 * value^2 / 1000000 + 0.015 * value. Coefficient 0.06571441 is taken verbatim from the TRO's own calculator source (https://nt.gov.au/property/home-owner-assistance/js/calculators.js, function duty_2017_18) and is confirmed by the TRO's published worked example ($140,000 -> $3,388 exactly). NOTE: the text layer of the I-SD-002 PDF renders this coefficient as '0.06574141' (digits transposed by PDF extraction); 0.06574141 would give $3,388.53 on the TRO's own example and is therefore wrong. The TRO calculator applies this band to values up to and including $525,000.

'Where the dutiable value exceeds $525 000 but is less than $3 million, the duty is 4.95 per cent of the amount.' FLAT - 4.95% of the ENTIRE dutiable value, not marginal. Confirmed by TRO calculator: 'var y = 0.0495*dutiableAmount' returned for '525000.01 <= dutiableAmount && 2999999.99 >= dutiableAmount'.

'Where the dutiable amount exceeds $3 million but is less than $5 million, the duty is 5.75 per cent of the dutiable amount.' FLAT - 5.75% of the ENTIRE dutiable value. Confirmed by TRO calculator: 'var z = 0.0575*dutiableAmount' returned for '3000000.00 <= dutiableAmount && 4999999.99 >= dutiableAmount'. (The I-SD-002 PDF text layer garbles the lower bound of this row as '$5 million'; the $3 million boundary is taken from the TRO calculator's own condition.)

'Where the dutiable amount is $5 million or more, duty is 5.95 per cent of the dutiable amount.' FLAT - 5.95% of the ENTIRE dutiable value. Confirmed by TRO calculator: 'var a = 0.0595*dutiableAmount' returned as the final else branch (i.e. dutiableAmount >= $5,000,000).

NT.landTaxSurcharges: None - there is no land tax in the Northern Territory, so there are no trust, absentee, foreign-owner or vacant-land land tax surcharges. Separately, and importantly for a developer buying through a company or trust: the NT also has NO foreign purchaser / additional foreign acquirer stamp duty surcharge. NT and the ACT are the only Australian jurisdictions with no foreign buyer duty surcharge, so a foreign-owned company or trust pays the same general conveyance rates transcribed above. I could not find any TRO page imposing a surcharge, and the TRO stamp duty page lists only exemptions and concessions (charities/exempt entities, house and land packages, electric vehicles, motor vehicle family transfers) with no surcharge provisions. Note also that the NT's Property Activation Levy (a levy on unused/vacant CBD land, which was the nearest thing to a vacant land holding charge) ceased from the 2022-23 financial year per the 2022-23 Budget measures.
unresolved: CRITICAL - BAND 1 IS NOT LINEAR. The NT's bottom duty band ($0 to $525,000) is a QUADRATIC formula, not a fixed+rate marginal band, and it cannot be represented by this schema's fixed/rate fields. I set fixed=0 and rate=0 on that band ON PURPOSE so that a naive implementation returns $0 and fails visibly, rather than silently producing a plausible but wrong figure. The band MUST be implemented from the formula in its rowText: V = value/1000; duty = 0.06571441*V*V + 15*V. Any NT feasibility calculation for a site under $525,000 that uses the bands array as fixed+rate will be wrong.

Bands 2, 3 and 4 are FLAT, not marginal - the rate applies to the whole dutiable value. This is unusual and easy to get wrong: a $3,000,000 site attracts 5.75% of $3,000,000 = $172,500, NOT 4.95% up to $3M plus a marginal top-up. Because the bands are flat there are genuine cliff-edge discontinuities at $3,000,000 (duty jumps from $148,500 at $2,999,999 to $172,500) and at $5,000,000 (jumps from $287,500 to $297,500). Confirm this cliff behaviour against the TRO calculator before relying on it for an acquisition decision near those thresholds - it materially changes the viability of a deal priced just over a threshold.

The Territory Revenue Office does NOT publish the conveyance rate table as a rendered HTML table anywhere on treasury.nt.gov.au or nt.gov.au. Both the TRO stamp duty page and the nt.gov.au 'Examples of duty and rates' page decline to state the rates and instead link to a JavaScript calculator. I therefore reconstructed the schedule from two primary sources and cross-validated them: (a) the TRO's own calculator source code at https://nt.gov.au/property/home-owner-assistance/js/calculators.js, function duty_2017_18, reached via createCalculator case 'SDC' -> createSDC -> sdConv -> sdConv_2017_18 (the general, no-concession path); and (b) TRO information sheet I-SD-002 'Stamp duty on business property and rights' (updated August 2019) at https://treasury.nt.gov.au/pms/tro/information/I-SD-002.pdf. The I-SD-002 PDF's extracted text is materially garbled in the rate section - it renders the formula coefficient as '0.06574141' (transposed digits), the band-2 lower bound as '$255 000', and the band-3 lower bound as '$5 million but is less than $5 million'. I resolved every one of these against the TRO calculator source and against the TRO's own worked-example arithmetic. Do not re-read that PDF's text layer as authoritative; the numbers transcribed here come from the calculator code plus arithmetic validation.

The worked example recorded in dutyExampleValue/dutyExampleDuty ($140,000 dutiable -> $3,388) is from TRO information sheet I-SD-002 and concerns BUSINESS property (goodwill plus plant and equipment), not land. I used it because I-SD-002 applies the identical general conveyance rate formula and it is the only worked example the TRO publishes for that formula - and it validates the coefficient exactly (0.06571441 * 140^2 + 15 * 140 = 1288.00 + 2100 = 3388.00). But it is NOT a land purchase example, and the TRO publishes no worked example for a land conveyance at any value. Note also that since 9 May 2023 duty on non-land business property has been abolished, so this example's own facts would no longer be dutiable - only its arithmetic is being relied on.

dutyMinimum is recorded as 0 because I could not confirm any minimum conveyance duty from a primary source. The TRO calculator simply floors the result at zero. I was unable to read Schedule 1 of the Stamp Duty Act 1978 to check for a statutory minimum: legislation.nt.gov.au serves the Act only as a PDF/Word download behind an API endpoint, and the outbound proxy returned HTTP 403 on that endpoint, so I could not verify the legislated rate table or any minimum-duty provision directly. If a minimum exists it would only matter for very low-value transfers.

The TRO calculator rounds the computed duty DOWN to the nearest 5 cents (functions flr2 then flr in calculators.js). This is immaterial at multi-million-dollar values but will cause small mismatches against the official calculator if not replicated.

The absence of an NT foreign purchaser duty surcharge is an inference from the absence of any such provision on TRO pages, not an explicit TRO statement that none exists. Given the user is buying through a company or trust that may be foreign-owned, this is worth a direct confirmation with the TRO (1300 305 353) before committing, since it is a negative finding rather than a positive one.

dutyPremiumThreshold is recorded as 5000000, the point at which the top 5.95% rate begins. The NT does not use the term 'premium rate' - it simply has flat rate tiers - so treat this field as 'top tier threshold' rather than a distinct premium duty.

taxYear is recorded as 2026-27 (the NT financial year current at the date of research, 5 August 2026). The rates themselves are not annually indexed and have applied since 1 July 2017, so the year label reflects when this was checked rather than a year-specific schedule.

landTaxThreshold is recorded as 0 and landTaxBands as an empty array purely because no land tax exists in the NT. Do not interpret a zero threshold as meaning all land is taxable from the first dollar - it means the tax does not exist. The consuming code should treat NT land tax as structurally absent.

NSW.warrantyName: Home Building Compensation (HBC) cover, provided through the Home Building Compensation Fund (HBCF) under the Home Building Act 1989 (NSW) and Home Building Regulation 2014
NSW.warrantyRegulator: State Insurance Regulatory Authority (SIRA) is the scheme regulator; icare HBCF is the sole government insurer/underwriter and sets the filed premium rates
NSW.contribMechanism: Two stacked layers. (1) Local infrastructure contributions to councils under s7.11 (contributions with nexus) or s7.12 (fixed percentage-of-cost levy) of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979, imposed via a council contributions plan; planning agreements under s7.4-7.10 are a negotiated third option. (2) A separate State-level Housing and Productivity Contribution (HPC) under a Ministerial planning order made under Part 7 Div 7.1 of the EP&A Act, applying in Greater Sydney, Central Coast, Illawarra-Shoalhaven and Lower Hunter/Greater Newcastle, plus add-on Transport Project Components (Pyrmont Peninsula, Aerotropolis station precincts) and Strategic Biodiversity Components (Cumberland Plain Conservation Plan, West Dapto, Western Sydney Growth Areas). From 1 July 2026 the Western Sydney Growth Areas and Aerotropolis Special Infrastructure Contributions (SICs) were folded into the HPC.
NSW.practitionerName: Registered design practitioner, principal design practitioner and registered building practitioner under the Design and Building Practitioners Act 2020 (NSW) and Design and Building Practitioners Regulation 2021 - regulated designs plus design compliance declarations and a building compliance declaration are mandatory for building work on class 2, 3 and 9c buildings (registered professional engineers under the same Act are a parallel requirement)
quirks: HBCF does NOT cover the apartment product most developers care about: construction of new multi-unit buildings with a rise in storeys of more than 3 is expressly exempt (SIRA exemptions page, Home Building Regulation 2014). So a 5-storey apartment block needs no HBC cover at all, while a 3-storey walk-up does - and pays the punishing H03 rate.

icare's filed HBCF base rates are wildly non-linear by construction code (metro, incl. GST and stamp duty, from 1 Nov 2025): H01 new dwelling 1.158%; H04 work to existing dwelling 1.111%; H05 swimming pools 0.596%; H02 work to an existing residential apartment building 4.935%; H03 new residential apartment building 13.503%. Rural postcodes get a 20% discount. Each builder then carries an individual actuarial loading or discount on top, so the actual premium is builder-risk-rated, not a fixed schedule.

There is a maximum liability cap of $340,000 per certificate of insurance (Home Building Regulation 2014), and premium is charged per certificate - a townhouse row can generate one certificate per dwelling. The cap is what makes the 13.5% H03 rate survivable on a large contract.

Developers of new strata buildings of 4 or more storeys must lodge a Strata Building Bond of 2% of the total construction contract price with the Secretary before an occupation certificate is issued, under Part 11 of the Strata Schemes Management Act 2015 (Strata Building Bond and Inspections Scheme). This sits alongside, not instead of, HBCF and is a real cash-flow item held for around 2 years pending interim and final defect inspections.

The Residential Apartment Buildings (Compliance and Enforcement Powers) Act 2020 requires developers of class 2 buildings to notify the Building Commissioner 6-12 months before applying for an occupation certificate, and gives the regulator power to issue prohibition orders blocking the OC or the registration of the strata plan, plus building work rectification orders. This is an existential settlement-risk item unique to NSW.

The DBP Act 2020 s37 statutory duty of care runs to owners and successors in title, applies retrospectively to work in the 10 years before commencement, and cannot be contracted out of - it has been read broadly by the courts to catch developers and individual company officers, not just builders.

The state HPC is charged on top of council s7.11/s7.12 contributions, not in substitution. Indexed base component as at 1 July 2026: Greater Sydney $13,000.73 per new dwelling lot (subdivision) and $10,833.94 per new medium/high-density dwelling; Central Coast, Illawarra-Shoalhaven and Lower Hunter $8,667.15 / $6,500.36. Rates are indexed quarterly to the Producer Price Index (Road and Bridge Construction - NSW), so a feasibility must escalate them.

Add-on HPC components can dwarf the base: Pyrmont Peninsula Transport Project Component $16,250.91 per dwelling, Cumberland Plain Conservation Plan Strategic Biodiversity Component $10,324.81 per dwelling/lot, Aerotropolis Station Precincts $8,148 per dwelling. Stacking base + transport + biodiversity is possible.

s7.12 levies are rate-capped by the EP&A Regulation: nil where development cost is $100,000 or less, max 0.5% for $100,001-$200,000, max 1% above $200,000 - but individual councils can and do hold Minister-approved higher maximums of 2% or 3%, listed in the Regulation. You must check the specific council's approved rate, not assume 1%.

s7.11 contributions are capped at $20,000 per lot or dwelling ($30,000 in identified greenfield/urban release areas) unless the council has an IPART-reviewed contributions plan, in which case the cap does not bind. Whether the site sits under a reviewed plan swings the per-dwelling number by tens of thousands.

HBCF exemptions have been carved out for build-to-rent schemes (cl 59B, from 2 March 2023), recognised housing providers/registered charities (cl 59A), council developers (cl 59C) and public sector agencies (s103E) - the delivery vehicle you choose changes whether the premium line exists at all. Reliance on several of these must be stated in the contract.

HPC obligations can be discharged by works-in-kind under the HPC Works-in-Kind Guideline, but only through competitive nomination rounds (1 June-31 August and 1 November-31 January) against Infrastructure Opportunities Plans, with Ministerial approval - it is a scheduled process, not an ad hoc negotiation.

Legislative regime in flux: the Building (Approvals and Practitioners) Bill 2026 has been introduced to restructure the NSW building approvals and certification regime (including removing existing construction and occupation certificate requirements and bringing prefabricated buildings into scope), following the 2025 Parliamentary review of the DBP and RAB Acts and the Building Legislation Amendment Act. Assume the practitioner and certification framework will shift within the feasibility horizon.

VIC.warrantyName: Home Warranty insurance (the First-resort Home Warranty Scheme), the statutory insurance scheme under Part 9A of the Building Act 1993 (Vic), introduced by the Building Legislation Amendment (Buyer Protections) Act 2025 and commenced 1 July 2026. It REPLACED Domestic Building Insurance (DBI) for contracts signed on or after 1 July 2026; DBI policies for earlier contracts continue on their original last-resort terms ($300,000 cap).
VIC.warrantyRegulator: Building and Plumbing Commission (BPC) — the sole provider and regulator. BPC was established 1 July 2025 and absorbed the Victorian Building Authority (VBA), Domestic Building Dispute Resolution Victoria (DBDRV) and the domestic building insurance arm of the Victorian Managed Insurance Authority (VMIA). Premiums are set by a Premiums Order gazetted under the Building Act 1993 and require ministerial approval before any change.
VIC.contribMechanism:
Four separate, cumulative mechanisms — a Victorian project can be hit by all of them at once:

1. GAIC (Growth Areas Infrastructure Contribution) — Part 9B of the Planning and Environment Act 1987. A one-off STATE charge per hectare in the 7 designated growth councils (Cardinia, Casey, Hume, Melton, Mitchell, Whittlesea, Wyndham), collected by the State Revenue Office. 2026-27 rates: Type A land $122,260/ha; Type B-1, B-2 and C land $145,220/ha. Deferral available at 5.6063% interest (2026-27); building works below the $1,528,532 threshold (2026-27) are an "excluded event". Can be satisfied by a work-in-kind (WIK) agreement negotiated with the VPA.

2. DCP (Development Contributions Plan) — Part 3B of the P&E Act 1987, applied as a schedule to clause 45.06 (Development Contributions Plan Overlay). Two levies: a Development Infrastructure Levy (DIL), which is UNCAPPED and set by the planning authority from apportioned infrastructure cost; and a Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL), capped by s46L at $1,590 per dwelling for 2026-27 (indexed 1 July annually by the ABS PPI for non-residential building construction in Victoria).

3. ICP (Infrastructure Contributions Plan) — clause 45.11 (Infrastructure Contributions Overlay), used in the same 7 growth councils. 2026-27 residential standard levy is $275,261 per net developable hectare ($119,682 community and recreation + $155,579 transport), plus optional bespoke supplementary levies and a land component (inner public purpose land plus land equalisation amounts).

4. Public open space contribution — s18 of the Subdivision Act 1988: up to 5% of the land or 5% of site value by default, but the VPA's Precinct Structure Planning guidelines recommend and many planning schemes (schedule to clause 53.01) require 10%. Triggered on most residential subdivisions of 3 or more lots.

Plus voluntary s173 agreements under the P&E Act as an alternative/supplement.
VIC.practitionerName: Registered Building Practitioner — Domestic Builder (Unlimited) (DB-U), registered with the Building and Plumbing Commission under the Building Act 1993. From 1 July 2026 a registered domestic builder must ALSO satisfy the new Minimum Financial Requirements (MFR) and hold an approved Maximum Construction Capacity (MCC), which replaced the old DBI eligibility / letter-of-eligibility assessment. Builders with an active DBI Letter of Eligibility on 30 June 2026 transitioned automatically, with their prior approved limit becoming their MCC.
quirks: REGIME CHANGE ON 1 JULY 2026 — do not use pre-2026 Victorian data. Domestic Building Insurance (DBI) was replaced by Home Warranty for all major domestic building contracts signed on or after 1 July 2026. The compulsory threshold rose from $16,000 to more than $20,000, the cover cap rose from $300,000 to $400,000 per home, and the scheme changed from LAST resort to FIRST resort. Many commercial sites (including insurance brokers) still publish the old $16,000 / $300,000 / last-resort figures.

FIRST RESORT is the big commercial difference. Under DBI a homeowner could only claim if the builder died, disappeared, became insolvent or failed to comply with a tribunal order. Under Home Warranty a homeowner can claim for incomplete, defective or non-compliant work while the builder is still trading and solvent, if the builder is unable or unwilling to fix it. A builder who refuses to respond to BPC on a rectification order can also be barred from the industry. This materially raises builder exposure and is the reason premiums are expected to sit above historic DBI levels.

THE THREE-STOREY CLIFF. Home Warranty only covers residential buildings up to three storeys. Apartment buildings of four storeys or more containing more than 2 homes have NO statutory warranty insurance in Victoria at all. Government's stated reason is to keep premiums low by excluding the high rectification cost of taller structures. A developer moving from a 3-storey to a 4-storey scheme crosses into an entirely different (and currently thinner) consumer-protection regime.

DEVELOPER BOND SCHEME — the Class 2 substitute, and a real cash-flow item. Developers of residential apartment buildings four storeys and above must lodge a bond of 2% of total build cost with BPC before applying for an occupancy permit. Owners can claim against it for defect rectification. It is an alternative to decennial insurance. Critically, the Building (Developer Bonds) Regulations 2026 exempt buildings whose building permit was issued before 1 July 2027, so in practice the scheme bites only on permits issued from 1 July 2027 onward. Exemptions also cover eligible build-to-rent developments (as defined in the Land Tax Act 2005), Homes Victoria projects, and registered agencies, in each case where a majority of lots will not be offered for sale.

OFF-THE-PLAN RESCISSION RISK tied to the bond. Once the bond scheme applies, a purchaser of an off-the-plan apartment is entitled to rescind their contract if the developer has not paid the bond, or has paid less than the required amount. This turns a bond administration slip into a pre-sale-destroying event, so bond compliance must be tracked as a sales risk, not just a permit condition.

MAXIMUM CONSTRUCTION CAPACITY (MCC) caps your pipeline, not just each job. From 1 July 2026 the Minimum Financial Requirements regime determines the total value of domestic building work a registered builder may have under construction at any one time. Staging and settlement timing must be modelled against the MCC, and BPC may reassess financial capacity when a builder seeks an MCC increase, breaches registration conditions, provides updated financials, or BPC initiates a review.

RECTIFICATION ORDERS REACH DEVELOPERS, NOT JUST BUILDERS. BPC can issue rectification orders directing builders, subcontractors AND developers to fix poor work at any time during construction and for up to 10 years after practical completion. This 10-year tail on the developer entity itself is unusual and survives the 6-year major-defect / 2-year other-defect Home Warranty claim windows.

MAJOR DEFECTS now expressly include waterproofing and weatherproofing, not just structural defects, and carry the 6-year cover period. Everything else gets 2 years. Minor cosmetic differences between the completed work and the contract plans and specifications are excluded, with BPC empowered to publish determinations on what counts as minor cosmetic.

GAIC is a per-HECTARE state charge, not a per-dwelling one, so its per-dwelling impact is driven entirely by yield. It is triggered by events such as land transfer, subdivision or a building permit. Deferral is available but accrues interest daily at the 10-year TCV bond rate (5.6063% for 2026-27). Work-in-kind agreements with the VPA can offset all or part of the liability and are worth negotiating early, since two model WIK agreements and guidelines are published.

GAIC BUILDING WORKS THRESHOLD. Building works on land inside a contribution area that cost below the statutory threshold ($1,528,532 for 2026-27, CPI-indexed) are an excluded GAIC event. Sequencing modest works below this threshold can avoid triggering liability.

OPEN SPACE CONTRIBUTION IS OFTEN 10%, NOT 5%. The Subdivision Act 1988 default is up to 5% of land or site value, but VPA Precinct Structure Planning guidelines recommend and many planning schemes mandate 10% via the schedule to clause 53.01. On a high-value infill site this single line item can dwarf the DCP levies. You must read the specific council's clause 53.01 schedule.

THE COMMUNITY INFRASTRUCTURE LEVY CAP IS NOT THE WHOLE DCP. The $1,590/dwelling CIL cap is widely misquoted as 'the DCP cap'. The Development Infrastructure Levy sitting alongside it is completely uncapped and is usually the far larger number.

CLADDING LEVY REPEALED AND REPLACED. Cladding Safety Victoria was wound up by the Cladding Safety Victoria Repeal Act 2026 and the Cladding Rectification Levy component of the Building Permit Levy was repealed. It was replaced by a new Building Permit Levy component applying only to certain building types in NON-REGIONAL Victoria where the cost of building works is $1.5 million or more, in force up to and including 30 June 2029, to fund BPC.

BUILDING MANUAL mandatory for new Class 1b, 2 and 3 buildings from 1 February 2027 — a single document covering design, construction and subsequent works, which the owner or owners corporation must keep and update annually. Buildings constructed before that date are unaffected. Small owner-operated Class 1b guest houses and B&Bs meeting certain criteria are exempt.

MORE CHANGE STILL COMING. The Building and Plumbing Administration and Enforcement Act 2026 (assented 19 May 2026) will become the new principal Act, commencing mid-to-late 2027 and no later than 1 December 2027. It brings new civil penalties, improvement notices, broader infringement powers and an expanded ability to make DIRECTORS personally liable in serious cases. An expert panel is separately advising on a framework for a wholly new Building Act. Assume Victorian settings will move again within the feasibility horizon.

PREMIUM IS PAID BY THE BUILDER TO BPC, on a tight clock: before the earlier of 10 business days after the contract is signed, or the work starting. Failure is an offence. But because it is a statutory scheme, the homeowner may still be protected even if the builder never paid — so non-payment creates builder liability without giving the developer any insurance saving.

An Insurance Information Statement (the way to check whether a Notice of Cover exists on a property, when cover ends and the maximum available) costs a non-refundable $51.80, payable even if no Notice of Cover is found. Relevant to due diligence on acquiring part-built or recently-built stock.

GAIC applies only in the 7 designated growth councils and ICPs only in the same 7. Infill and established-area projects escape both entirely, which is why the honest per-dwelling contribution range is so wide — a greenfield Wyndham lot and a Yarra infill apartment are in effectively different contribution regimes.

The upper end of my practitioner cost range includes non-regulatory costs I could not verify from primary sources — commercial registration-preparation courses (advertised by third parties around $6,500-$7,000) and accountant-prepared financial reports for the Minimum Financial Requirements assessment. hasClass2Regime IS A JUDGEMENT CALL AND SHOULD BE REVIEWED. I set it TRUE because Victoria's Developer Bond Scheme imposes a distinct, additional, quantified regulated cost (2% of total build cost) specifically on multi-unit apartment buildings of four storeys and above, which no other building work bears — plus the Class 1b/2/3 building manual obligation from 1 February 2027. But note three genuine caveats: (i) the bond does not effectively commence until building permits issued from 1 July 2027, so it is NOT yet an operative cost as at August 2026; (ii) a bond is refundable capital, so its true economic cost is the cost of the money plus any defect drawdown, not the full 2%; (iii) the MECHANISM is NOT the NSW one — Victoria does NOT have NSW-style registered design practitioners lodging regulated design declarations. If your criterion is strictly the NSW design-declaration mechanism, set this FALSE. If it is 'a distinct additional regulated compliance cost on Class 2 work', TRUE is correct.

The 2% developer bond is described in primary Victorian Government material as 2% of 'total build cost', but I did NOT read the Building (Developer Bonds) Regulations 2026 directly, so the precise statutory definition of build cost, the bond form (cash vs bank guarantee), the release and drawdown mechanics, and the timing of any residual return are unconfirmed. These determine the real carrying cost and should be checked in the regulations before modelling.

The four-storey threshold for the developer bond, and the corresponding three-storey ceiling on Home Warranty, are confirmed in narrative form from Planning Victoria, Engage Victoria and BPC. The exact statutory definition of storeys, and how mixed-use or podium/basement configurations are counted, is NOT confirmed. This matters because the whole regime flips at that line.

REPORTED BUT NOT PRIMARY-CONFIRMED: consumer rights to exit a domestic building contract where completion time blows out by more than 50% or costs rise by more than 15%, apparently under the Domestic Building Contracts Amendment Act 2025. I saw this only in secondary and social-media sources attributed to BPC and could not verify it against the Act or BPC guidance. If real it is a significant developer/builder risk and should be confirmed.

Whether Victoria's 'expanded building industry registration' reform (new registration categories for building consultants and site supervisors, and renaming of draftsperson and project management categories) has commenced is unconfirmed. Planning Victoria describes it in future tense, with regulations still subject to consultation and impact assessment. No new registration cost from this reform is included in my figures.

QLD.warrantyName: Queensland Home Warranty Scheme (statutory insurance under the Queensland Building and Construction Commission Act 1991 and the QBCC Regulation 2018) - commonly called QBCC home warranty insurance
QLD.warrantyRegulator: Queensland Building and Construction Commission (QBCC) - the scheme is a not-for-profit statutory insurance fund administered by QBCC itself, not by private insurers
QLD.contribMechanism: Infrastructure charges: levied by an infrastructure charges notice (Planning Act 2016 (Qld) ch 4, notice under s 119/s 121) at rates set in each local government's adopted infrastructure charges resolution (charges resolution). An adopted charge cannot exceed the "maximum adopted charge" / prescribed amount in sch 16 of the Planning Regulation 2017, indexed annually by the Producer Price Index for road and bridge construction in Queensland (currently reported by councils at $36,670.70 per dwelling house of 3 or more bedrooms; lower prescribed amounts for 1-2 bedroom dwellings and multiple dwellings). Charges are per-unit-of-demand (per dwelling / per bedroom band), not per-value, and are offset by credits for existing lawful use. Councils may also enter infrastructure agreements, and must give offsets/refunds where a developer builds trunk infrastructure identified in the LGIP (local government infrastructure plan). In South East Queensland, the water supply and sewerage component is levied separately by the distributor-retailer (Urban Utilities, Unitywater) under its Water Netserv Plan / Infrastructure Charges Schedule pursuant to the South-East Queensland Water (Distribution and Retail Restructuring) Act 2009 - so a SEQ developer receives two charges notices, and the combined amount is what the sch 16 cap constrains. Outside SEQ the council levies the water/sewer component itself.
QLD.practitionerName: QBCC contractor licence (Builder - Low Rise / Medium Rise / Open) plus, for engineering design, mandatory Registered Professional Engineer of Queensland (RPEQ) registration under the Professional Engineers Act 2002. There is no Queensland analogue of the NSW registered-design-practitioner / regulated-design-declaration regime.
quirks: Three-storey cliff-edge on home warranty cover: building work in or for a multiple dwelling of MORE than three storeys (disregarding one storey used mainly as a carpark) is not 'residential construction work' and is therefore NOT insurable under the QHWS. A 3-storey walk-up carries the premium and the statutory cover; a 4-storey apartment building carries neither. Purchasers of the taller building have no scheme fallback, which changes the risk/warranty story for buyers, financiers and the developer's own contract security.

Premium is a pre-condition to starting: the contractor must pay the QHWS premium to QBCC before commencing work and, in practice, before accepting a deposit - it is a genuine up-front cash outflow, not an end-of-job cost, and it must be shown in the contract price.

Cover is capped at $200,000 per dwelling for non-completion/defect claims, and the structural-defect cover period runs 6 years 6 months from the date of contract (extending to 7 years where the build takes more than 6 months) - the clock runs from contract date, not practical completion, which is unusual.

Mandatory RPEQ: under the Professional Engineers Act 2002 all 'professional engineering services' provided in or for Queensland must be carried out or directly supervised by a Registered Professional Engineer of Queensland. Interstate consulting engineers cannot simply sign Queensland designs - this is a Queensland-only registration cost and scheduling constraint.

Two infrastructure charges notices in SEQ: council levies transport/parks/stormwater, while Urban Utilities or Unitywater separately levies water and sewerage under the SEQ Water (Distribution and Retail Restructuring) Act 2009. Feasibility models built on 'the council charge' alone systematically understate SEQ per-dwelling contributions.

Charges are capped by state regulation (sch 16, Planning Regulation 2017) - unlike NSW s7.11 plans there is a hard statutory ceiling per dwelling, and many regional councils adopt well below it or run temporary discounts/incentive policies down to near zero, so the same product can face a 10x swing in contributions between LGAs.

Infrastructure charges notices are negotiable and appellable: a recipient can seek a negotiated infrastructure charges notice, and can appeal a charges notice to the Planning and Environment Court or a development tribunal on limited grounds (e.g. error in calculation or application of the resolution). Offsets and refunds for trunk infrastructure delivered by the developer are a statutory entitlement, not a favour.

Third-party (submitter) merits appeals: for impact-assessable development, anyone who made a properly made submission can appeal an approval to the Planning and Environment Court. This open-standing merits appeal right is a Queensland hallmark and a real programme/holding-cost risk that NSW and Victorian developers do not face in the same way.

Deemed approval: if the assessment manager fails to decide a code-assessable application within the statutory period, the applicant may give a deemed approval notice under the Planning Act 2016 and obtain approval by operation of law - a genuine tactical lever unique among the states.

Statutory trust accounts: the Building Industry Fairness (Security of Payment) Act 2017 requires project trust accounts and retention trust accounts on eligible building contracts, currently at a $10 million private-sector threshold. The planned reduction to $3m (from 1 March 2025) and $1m (from 1 October 2025) was paused indefinitely by proclamation on 31 January 2025 - but it remains on the books and is the single most likely near-term cost/administration shock for QLD builders.

QBCC Minimum Financial Requirements: licensees must hold and evidence net tangible assets and current ratio against a declared Maximum Revenue, with annual (and category-dependent) accountant-prepared reporting. Exceeding declared maximum revenue is itself a licence breach - so a developer's chosen builder can be legally incapable of taking on the contract even if commercially willing.

Combustible cladding: Building Regulation 2006 imposes the Safer Buildings combustible cladding checklist regime on private Class 2-9 buildings of 2 or more storeys built or re-clad between 1994 and 2018 - a due-diligence and remediation liability that attaches on acquisition of existing stock.

Building certification is privatised and licensed separately: private building certifiers licensed by QBCC under the Building Act 1975 issue development permits for building work, and are subject to their own conflict-of-interest rules. The Queensland Development Code (QDC) sits alongside the NCC with Queensland-specific mandatory parts (e.g. sustainable buildings, pool safety, on-site sewerage).

Multi-unit product almost always requires a community titles scheme under the Body Corporate and Community Management Act 1997, with regulation-module selection (Standard, Accommodation, Small Schemes, Commercial) locked in at establishment - a decision with long-tail consequences for on-sale and letting arrangements.

State referral overlays bite hard: SDAP (State Development Assessment Provisions) referral to the State Assessment and Referral Agency, plus SEQ koala habitat mapping, state-controlled road access, vegetation management and flood/erosion-prone overlays, frequently drive redesign on sites that would be clean in other states.
