SA.warrantyName: Building Indemnity Insurance (required under s 34 of the Building Work Contractors Act 1995 (SA) and the Building Work Contractors Regulations 2011)
SA.warrantyRegulator: Consumer and Business Services (CBS), SA Attorney-General's Department — licensing, eligibility and enforcement; cover is written by private insurers (QBE holds the large majority of the SA market) and reinsured/backed by the South Australian Government Financing Authority (SAFA), which administers the scheme's builder/broker, homeowner and certifier interfaces
SA.contribMechanism: SA has no NSW-style s7.11/s7.12 general developer-contributions system and no GAIC equivalent. Instead a developer faces a stack of separate, mostly state-level charges: (1) OPEN SPACE CONTRIBUTION under s 198 of the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act 2016 (PDI Act), with rates set by the Planning, Development and Infrastructure (Fees, Charges and Contributions) Regulations 2019 — either up to 12.5% of the relevant area vested as open space (available where a division creates more than 20 allotments with one or more under 1 ha) or a prescribed cash contribution per additional allotment/community or strata lot not exceeding 1 ha, paid into the Planning and Development Fund (indicatively ~$7,253 per allotment for Metropolitan Adelaide, lower in regional SA, indexed ~1 July); (2) SA WATER AUGMENTATION CHARGES under the Water Industry Act 2012 pricing/developer-charges policy — in 2025-26, $10,240 per new residential greenfield allotment in the Greater Adelaide Region ($5,120 water + $5,120 wastewater) and $5,120 per additional infill connection ($2,560 + $2,560), on an announced escalation path toward roughly $10,000 for infill from 1 July 2027, plus any headworks/network extension the developer must fund directly; (3) INFRASTRUCTURE SCHEMES under Part 13 of the PDI Act — 'basic infrastructure schemes' in declared designated growth areas, funded by scheme contributions and charges on land (Subdivisions 7 and 8); the first, the Concordia Basic Infrastructure Scheme, sets a local infrastructure charge of $15,409 per dwelling for residential development and $272,425 per net developable hectare for employment land. 'General infrastructure schemes' exist in the Act but are not yet operative (they require a State Planning Commission inquiry and report first). Councils also commonly impose land-division infrastructure/asset requirements and one-off deeds/land management agreements, and the Affordable Housing Overlay's 15% affordable-housing requirement (developments of 20+ dwellings/allotments in overlay areas) functions as a de facto in-kind contribution. Honest per-dwelling total: very roughly $4,000 for a simple infill lot where only a partial water/wastewater charge bites, ~$15,000-$20,000 typical for a metropolitan infill or small greenfield lot (open space contribution plus SA Water augmentation), and $40,000+ per dwelling in a designated growth area carrying a basic infrastructure scheme charge on top.
SA.practitionerName: Building Work Contractor's Licence (company or individual) issued by Consumer and Business Services under the Building Work Contractors Act 1995, coupled with a nominated registered Building Work Supervisor, and a QBE/SAFA Letter of Eligibility for Building Indemnity Insurance (a practical precondition CBS requires before a contractor licence issues)
quirks: Building Indemnity Insurance thresholds and limits moved recently: from 10 November 2025 the trigger value rose from $12,000 to $20,000 and the statutory policy limit rose to $250,000 (QBE lifted its own limit to $250,000 from 1 October 2025). Feasibility models and contract templates built on the old $12,000 / $150,000 figures are now wrong.

BII cover is narrow by national standards - it responds only where the builder dies, disappears or becomes insolvent, and runs for 5 years from completion. It is not a general defects warranty, so buyer/lender due diligence in SA leans harder on the builder's own covenant.

SA's scheme is a private-market scheme sitting on a government balance sheet: QBE writes most policies, SAFA reinsures and administers the scheme's public-facing information, and CBS gates entry via eligibility letters and job/turnover profile limits. A builder's eligibility ceiling, not the contract, is often the binding constraint on how many dwellings can be under construction at once. (QBE-insured builders received a 9% uplift to eligibility and job-profile limits on 1 July 2026.)

There is no general council developer-contributions plan regime. A developer cannot look up a single 'contributions plan' the way they would in NSW or QLD - the charges are scattered across the PDI Act open space contribution, SA Water augmentation charges, and (in growth areas only) a Part 13 infrastructure scheme.

Part 13 infrastructure schemes are brand new and only just being used. Concordia is the first basic infrastructure scheme, at $15,409 per dwelling; 'general infrastructure schemes' remain dormant because the Act requires a State Planning Commission inquiry before they can be switched on. Expect more designated growth areas to acquire per-dwelling charges over the next few years - a greenfield feasibility done today can be repriced by a scheme declaration.

SA Water augmentation charges are on a deliberate, steep escalation path (infill went from $2,500 per connection in 2024-25 to $5,120 in 2025-26, heading toward about $10,000 from 1 July 2027). The charge attaches by SA Water development approval date within the financial year, so approval timing materially changes cost.

The open space contribution is per additional allotment and only bites on allotments not exceeding 1 hectare; a strata or community-title conversion can therefore attract it lot-by-lot. Above 20 allotments the authority can instead demand up to 12.5% of the site vested as open space, which is a land take, not a cash line item.

The Planning and Design Code's Affordable Housing Overlay requires a minimum 15% affordable housing in developments of 20 or more dwellings or residential allotments in overlay areas, and the overlay is routinely applied when land is rezoned for growth or higher density. Rezoning upside in SA is usually priced with a 15% affordable-housing haircut plus a referral to the housing authority.

Building consent can be issued by a private accredited building certifier or by the council, but SA layers on a mandatory notification/inspection regime and a Statement of Compliance (new form effective 5 April 2024) that must be signed and lodged with the consent authority at the same time as the notice of completion; a Certificate of Occupancy is required for all new buildings under the PDI Act, including houses. Missing paperwork stops occupation, not just settlement.

SA regulates trees more aggressively than most states through 'regulated' and 'significant' tree provisions - a single mature tree on or near a site can force redesign or a separate development approval, and native vegetation clearance triggers Significant Environmental Benefit offset payments under the Native Vegetation Act 1991, a cash cost with no direct equivalent in eastern-state infill work.

The state has an unusually centralised planning system: one Planning and Design Code statewide, assessment by accredited professionals or regional assessment panels, and a Minister/State Planning Commission with broad call-in and impact-assessed development powers. Local politics matters less than in NSW or VIC, but state policy shifts hit every council at once.

WA.warrantyName: Home Indemnity Insurance (compulsory under the Home Building Contracts Act 1991 (WA), Part 3A; policies issued by QBE Insurance (Australia) Ltd as agent for a State-supported scheme, plus AOBIS for owner-builders)
WA.warrantyRegulator: Building and Energy, Department of Local Government, Industry Regulation and Safety (LGIRS) — established 1 July 2025, taking over Industry Regulation and Safety from the former DEMIRS/DMIRS. Building Services Board handles registration; the permit authority (local government) must sight the HII certificate before issuing a building permit.
WA.contribMechanism: Development Contribution Plans (DCPs) applying to gazetted Development Contribution Areas (DCAs), imposed through local planning scheme provisions made under the Planning and Development Act 2005 and the Planning and Development (Local Planning Schemes) Regulations 2015, guided by State Planning Policy 3.6 – Infrastructure Contributions (revised SPP 3.6 gazetted 30 April 2021). Contributions are levied per lot/dwelling or per hectare of developable/net lettable area via an annually reviewed Cost Apportionment Schedule. Separate and additional: (a) public open space cession of 10% of gross subdivisible area, or cash-in-lieu valued under ss.153-155 of the Planning and Development Act 2005, imposed as a WAPC subdivision condition under WAPC Development Control Policy 2.3; (b) ad hoc WAPC/local government subdivision and development conditions for headworks, road upgrades and district infrastructure; (c) Metropolitan Region Improvement Tax (0.14% of aggregated taxable land value above $300,000 in the Perth metropolitan region) under the Metropolitan Region Improvement Tax Act 1959, which funds MRS reserve acquisition. There is no WA equivalent of Victoria's GAIC or a state-wide per-dwelling infrastructure charge.
WA.practitionerName: Building service provider registration (builder, building surveyor, painter) and building engineer registration under the Building Services (Registration) Act 2011 (WA) and Building Services (Registration) Regulations 2011 — a general licensing regime that applies to all building work, not a Class 2-specific declared-design regime. Structural and fire safety building engineer registration commenced 1 July 2024; civil and mechanical building engineer registration commenced 1 July 2025. WA has no counterpart to the NSW Design and Building Practitioners Act 2020: no registered design practitioners, no regulated design declarations, no compliance declarations and no 2% strata building bond for Class 2 work.
quirks: HOME INDEMNITY INSURANCE DOES NOT APPLY TO APARTMENTS. Under the Home Building Contracts (Home Indemnity Insurance Exemptions) Regulations 2002 (amended 2024), building work on a 'multi-storey multi-unit development' (a building of 2 or more independent dwelling units) is exempt from the compulsory HII requirement, provided the builder gives the prescribed notice to the owner in the prescribed manner and time. So a Perth apartment developer typically carries NO statutory warranty insurance cost at all, but must get the exemption notice mechanics exactly right — the notice requirements are precondition-heavy and getting them wrong reinstates the insurance obligation and exposes the builder to prosecution. Feasibility models built on eastern-states assumptions routinely over-state WA warranty cost for Class 2 and under-state the paperwork risk.

Cover limits doubled in 2024: HII now pays up to $40,000 for loss of deposit and up to $200,000 for incomplete or defective work (previously $20,000/$100,000), capped at the contract value, with a $500 QBE excess. Cover runs for the construction period plus six years from practical completion, and triggers only on the builder's death, disappearance or insolvency (plus non-renewal/cancellation of registration on financial grounds) — not on mere refusal to rectify.

QBE is effectively the only provider for registered builders, writing as agent for the State scheme (the State receives a share of premiums). There is no published premium rate table: eligibility and per-project premiums are set by QBE underwriting on the builder's financial capacity, turnover and open-job limits. A thinly capitalised or new builder may be refused eligibility outright, which is a hard stop on the project, not just a cost line.

SUBDIVISION IS A STATE DECISION, NOT A COUNCIL ONE. The Western Australian Planning Commission (not the local government) determines all subdivision and strata subdivision applications under the Planning and Development Act 2005. Local government is a referral agency only. Developers must therefore run two parallel processes — WAPC for subdivision (including built-strata) and the local government/DAP for development approval — with different decision-makers, timeframes and appeal postures.

TWO LAYERS OF PLANNING SCHEME IN PERTH AND PEEL. The Metropolitan Region Scheme (and the Peel and Greater Bunbury region schemes) sits above local schemes and reserves land for regional roads, parks and infrastructure. Land in an MRS reservation cannot be developed and is compulsorily acquired over time, funded by the Metropolitan Region Improvement Tax. Due diligence must check the MRS reservation layer separately from the local scheme — a clean local zoning tells you nothing.

10% PUBLIC OPEN SPACE CESSION, FREE OF COST. WAPC Development Control Policy 2.3 requires 10% of the gross subdivisible area to be ceded free of cost and vested in the Crown as recreation reserve, generally where 6 or more lots are created (including built-strata). Cash-in-lieu is only available with WAPC agreement under s.153, valued by the Valuer-General or a licensed valuer under s.155 — so on infill sites this can be a five- or six-figure unbudgeted cash cost triggered purely by lot count.

TWO CONSTRUCTION LEVIES ON TOP OF PERMIT FEES. (1) Construction Training Fund levy at 0.2% of estimated construction value — payable before construction starts, on residential, commercial and civil work, and payable whether or not a building permit is required. The threshold rose from $20,000 to $100,000 for projects starting construction on or after 1 July 2026 (projects that started earlier stay on the $20,000 threshold). (2) Building Services Levy at 0.137% of estimated value (minimum $61.65 for values up to $45,000). Uncertified permits also attract a permit authority fee of about 0.32% (minimum $110).

DEVELOPMENT ASSESSMENT PANELS ARE NOW OPT-IN, NOT MANDATORY. Since the 1 March 2024 reforms (Planning and Development Amendment Act 2023), DAP determination is an election available to the applicant for non-excluded development over $2 million, including grouped and multiple dwellings of any size — it is no longer a compulsory diversion. Choosing a DAP over the council removes the elected-member politics but also removes the council's own appeal-avoidance incentives, so the pathway choice is a genuine strategic decision.

A PERMANENT STATE-LEVEL 'SIGNIFICANT DEVELOPMENT' PATHWAY. Part 11B of the Planning and Development Act 2005 (permanent, replacing the temporary COVID-era Part 17 which closed to new applications on 29 December 2023) lets a proponent apply directly to the WAPC for development approval where value exceeds $20 million in Perth and Peel or $5 million elsewhere in the State. It is optional and bypasses the local government entirely. Major developments over $10 million are automatically referred to a Design Review Panel.

R-CODES SPLIT INTO TWO VOLUMES. State Planning Policy 7.3 Residential Design Codes Volume 1 governs single houses and grouped dwellings; Volume 2 – Apartments governs apartment development in higher-density areas and activity centres and drives design review panel engagement and design-quality assessment. Volume 2 imposes real, chargeable design and design-review cost on apartment projects — but as a planning policy, not as a registered-practitioner declaration regime, so it does not create the NSW-style statutory compliance-declaration overhead.

BUILDING ENGINEERS MUST NOW BE REGISTERED. WA phased in mandatory registration of building engineers under the Building Services (Registration) Act 2011: structural and fire safety from 1 July 2024, civil and mechanical from 1 July 2025. This applies to prescribed areas of engineering for buildings under the Building Act 2011 and the NCC across all classes, so it narrows the pool of engineers who can sign WA work and can lengthen procurement — but it is not Class 2-specific.

MAJOR BUILDING REFORM IS LANDING NOW. The WA Government's December 2023 'landmark reforms' package (responding to the Building Confidence Report) has a first stage due to commence in 2026, including mandatory inspections of high-rise apartment buildings, tiered registration of builders, stricter design documentation requirements, third-party review of structural and fire safety designs for complex and significant buildings, and expanded Building Commissioner enforcement powers. A Class 2 project entering the pipeline now should be priced on the assumption that third-party design review becomes a real line item during its life. A separate review of WA's home building contract laws was announced on 2 July 2025.

OWNER-BUILDERS AND BUILDERS BUILDING FOR THEMSELVES FACE A DEFERRED, SALE-TRIGGERED INSURANCE OBLIGATION. An owner-builder does not need HII to build, but must obtain cover if the property is sold within seven years of the building permit being granted; a registered builder may seek an exemption for their own principal place of residence on the same seven-year sale condition. This traps 'build then flip' strategies that would be unremarkable elsewhere.

DCP RATES ARE PER-LOT AND ANNUALLY RE-STRUCK, SO YOUR CONTRIBUTION MOVES AFTER YOU BUY. Cost Apportionment Schedules are reviewed annually and gazetted per DCA. Outer-growth land-assembly cell arrangements are far heavier than community-infrastructure DCPs: City of Wanneroo East Wanneroo Cells infrastructure cost per lot ran roughly $18,000 (Cell 1 Ashby-Tapping), $26,805 (Cell 2 Sinagra), $22,275 (Cell 3 Wanneroo) and $29,947 (Cell 9 East Landsdale) in the 2024-25 review, while the Yanchep-Two Rocks community infrastructure DCP was only $3,909.23 per lot in 2021-22. Established infill suburbs with no gazetted DCA may attract nothing at all beyond POS and headworks. The revised SPP 3.6 also introduced a right of independent review to the State Administrative Tribunal, so DCP rates and cost schedules are now contestable.

TAS.warrantyName: None in force — Tasmania abolished compulsory housing indemnity / home warranty insurance in 2008 and is the only Australian state without a mandatory scheme. A replacement scheme is legislated by the Residential Building (Home Warranty Insurance Amendments) Act 2023 (No. 25 of 2023), which amends the Residential Building Work Contracts and Dispute Resolution Act 2016, but its operative provisions commence on a day to be proclaimed and had not been proclaimed as at the date of this research.
TAS.warrantyRegulator: None currently — no scheme is in force. Consumer, Building and Occupational Services (CBOS), Department of Justice (Tas) is the building/consumer regulator and would administer the legislated but uncommenced scheme. In the interim CBOS administers a discretionary, budget-funded Financial Assistance Package for consumers affected by construction company failures, which is a government safety net rather than insurance and creates no premium cost line for a builder or developer.
TAS.contribMechanism: Tasmania has no codified developer contributions system equivalent to NSW s7.11/s7.12 or Victorian DCPs/GAIC. Contributions arise from three separate, largely uncoordinated sources: (1) planning permit conditions and negotiated agreements under the Land Use Planning and Approvals Act 1993 (LUPAA) — Part 5 agreements between a developer and the planning authority, typically framed as "works internal" (infrastructure built at developer cost and gifted to the council) and "works external" (stand-alone assets such as pump stations or road upgrades at developer cost); (2) public open space contributions on subdivision under Part 3 of the Local Government (Building and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1993, ss 116-117 — a contribution of up to 5% of the subdivided land, or cash in lieu of up to 5% of land value calculated under s 117(2), generally triggered on subdivision into 3 or more lots (or a 2-lot subdivision where a lot is capable of further subdivision), with each council operating its own open space policy; and (3) TasWater developer charges (headworks charges) for water and sewerage — a statewide, single-authority regime set through the Tasmanian Economic Regulator's Water and Sewerage Price Determination, not by councils, with per-connection charges for a standard 20mm connection of approximately $3,025 water and $1,797 sewerage (about $4,800 combined) for 2026-27, scaled by connection size and credited for existing lots/connections. Subdivision approval is a separate LG(B&MP) Act sealing process running alongside the LUPAA planning permit. Tasmania is generally the lowest infrastructure-charge jurisdiction in Australia, with commonly cited averages around $5,000 per lot, but the total is highly site-specific because "works external" obligations and open space cash-in-lieu on high-value land can dominate.
TAS.practitionerName: Building practitioner accreditation and licensing under the Building Act 2016 (Tas) and the Occupational Licensing Act 2005 (Tas), administered by CBOS / the Director of Building Control. Practitioner categories include builder, building surveyor, building designer (three sub-classes graded by project complexity, each with minimum qualifications, supervised experience and professional indemnity insurance), engineer and plumber. Compliance documentation is the Certificate of Likely Compliance issued by an accredited building surveyor, with work sorted into Director-determined categories (low-risk, notifiable and permit work); permit work additionally requires a building permit from the council as permit authority. Tasmania has NO distinct additional regulated design-declaration regime for NCC Class 2 residential work. There is no analogue to the NSW Design and Building Practitioners Act 2020 — no separate registration of "design practitioners" for Class 2, no regulated design declarations, no compliance declarations lodged to a state portal, and no Class 2-specific occupation certificate audit or developer-rating scheme. Class 2 buildings attract higher-tier designer and building surveyor accreditation classes and a more demanding Certificate of Likely Compliance, but that is the ordinary complexity gradient of the general licensing system that applies to all building work, not a separate statutory overlay. hasClass2Regime is therefore false.
quirks: No mandatory home warranty / builder indemnity insurance. Tasmania abolished its compulsory scheme in 2008 and is the only Australian state without one. This removes a 0.5-2% of contract value cost line that exists in every other jurisdiction, but it also means purchaser and lender comfort rests entirely on the builder's own solvency, balance sheet and track record. Expect financiers and off-the-plan purchasers to demand substitute security — bank guarantees, retentions, parent company guarantees, or a voluntary policy — and price that into the deal rather than assuming a saving.

The replacement scheme is legislated but dormant. The Residential Building (Home Warranty Insurance Amendments) Act 2023 amends the Residential Building Work Contracts and Dispute Resolution Act 2016 to require a policy for residential building contracts over a proposed $20,000 threshold, with the homeowner as beneficiary, covering loss of deposit, non-completion and defects subject to caps where the builder dies, disappears or becomes insolvent. It commences by proclamation and remains uncommenced. Consultation material has floated premiums in the order of $1,600-$3,200 on a $400,000 contract (roughly 0.4-0.8%). Any feasibility spanning more than about 12 months should carry this as a contingent, not-yet-payable cost, and contracts should anticipate a mid-project commencement.

Water and sewerage headworks are set by ONE statewide authority, not by councils. TasWater is the sole water and sewerage corporation for the whole state (stormwater stays with councils), and its developer charges are approved by the Tasmanian Economic Regulator in a four-yearly Price and Service Plan / Price Determination. This makes headworks unusually predictable and uniform across Tasmania, but it also means a single regulatory decision can reset the charge statewide overnight. TasWater sought roughly a doubling of connection charges in the 2026-2030 determination; the Regulator cut it back to about $3,025 water and $1,797 sewerage for a 20mm connection from July 2026. Watch determination cycles as a step-change risk.

Section 56 LUPAA gives a route to strip stale headworks conditions. Where TasWater's developer charges policy has changed after a permit issued, a developer can apply to the council for a minor amendment under s 56 of LUPAA to remove or vary the TasWater permit conditions relating to headworks charges. On a long-dated or staged approval this is real money and is not obvious from the permit itself — always test whether an inherited permit is carrying superseded charges.

Subdivision runs on a separate statutory track from the planning permit. Beyond the LUPAA planning permit, subdivision in Tasmania is governed by Part 3 of the Local Government (Building and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1993 — a 1993-era conveyancing-flavoured regime for sealing of plans, engineering standards and open space. Two approvals, two sets of conditions, two failure points. Developers used to a single consolidated development consent routinely underestimate the sealing stage and its timing.

Public open space contribution is a percentage of LAND VALUE, not a fixed per-lot charge. Up to 5% of the land or its value under ss 116-117 of the LG(B&MP) Act 1993, generally on subdivision into 3+ lots, with each council setting its own policy and each valuing differently. On expensive Hobart, Kingborough or Clarence land this single line can exceed all other contributions combined, and it scales with land value rather than with dwelling count — the opposite of a per-dwelling levy.

Statutory warranties under the Residential Building Work Contracts and Dispute Resolution Act 2016 cannot be contracted out of, and disputes must go through COMPULSORY CBOS mediation first. A residential building dispute goes to CBOS mediation before it can reach TASCAT's Civil and Consumer Stream, and a mediation panel must cease if there is no settlement within 20 days. Budget for a mandatory pre-litigation step and the delay it imposes on defect resolution.

One statewide planning scheme with local variation only in a schedule. The Tasmanian Planning Scheme comprises State Planning Provisions (uniform zones and 16 codes statewide) plus a Local Provisions Schedule per council. Controls are far more standardised than in NSW or Victoria, but where the LPS overlays bite they are the only local lever — and Planning Directives (for example Planning Directive No. 5.1, Bushfire-Prone Areas Code) can change the statewide provisions directly without any council process.

Bushfire and landslip hazard overlays cover an unusually large share of developable land, and they operate twice. Statewide bushfire-prone area and landslip hazard overlay maps drive planning-stage requirements under the codes AND separate construction requirements under the Building Act 2016, typically forcing a bushfire attack level assessment, a bushfire hazard management plan by an accredited person, and hazard-area construction standards. On Tasmanian fringe and hillside sites this is a near-default cost and a design constraint on lot yield, not an exception.

Planning, building, environment and strata appeals all land in TASCAT. The former Resource Management and Planning Appeal Tribunal was folded into the Tasmanian Civil and Administrative Tribunal, so a single tribunal handles planning, building, environmental and strata title matters across separate streams. Third-party appeal rights on discretionary planning permits are real and are a live programme risk.

Foreign Investor Duty Surcharge at 8% on residential property, plus a foreign investor land tax surcharge — with a developer carve-out. Tasmanian-based foreign developers delivering at least 50 residential dwellings in Tasmania in a 12-month period can apply for relief from the surcharge. That 50-dwelling hurdle is a genuine structuring threshold: below it a foreign-owned entity wears the full 8%, above it the relief can be transformational for feasibility.

NT.warrantyName: Residential building cover — fidelity fund certificate (Building Act 1993 (NT), s 54C and following; Building Regulations 1993 (NT))
NT.warrantyRegulator: Building Advisory Services, NT Department of Lands, Planning and Environment (statutory scheme under the Building Act 1993); certificates issued by the approved fidelity fund, Fidelity Fund NT; builder registration and discipline by the NT Building Practitioners Board
NT.contribMechanism: "Developer contributions" made through a "contribution plan" under Part 6 (ss 67–72) of the Planning Act 1999 (NT), given effect through the Northern Territory Planning Scheme 2020 and levied as a condition of development consent by the Development Consent Authority, with the money collected for and spent by the relevant local government council or service authority. Unlike NSW s7.11/s7.12 or Queensland infrastructure charges, this is NOT a territory-wide charging regime: a contribution is payable only where a gazetted contribution plan covers the land, and the small number of plans that exist are narrow-purpose — stormwater drainage, roadworks and CBD car parking (s 70 deals specifically with car parking contributions). City of Darwin, City of Palmerston and Litchfield Council are the main councils with plans; rates are typically struck per square metre of site area or per car space rather than per dwelling (e.g. City of Darwin stormwater drainage 2024/25: Policy Area A $9.43/m2, Area B $5.76/m2, Area C $3.67/m2). Separately, and outside the Planning Act, headworks/extension charges for water, sewerage and electricity are levied by Power and Water Corporation under its Water and Sewerage Services Extension Policy (WASSEP) — for many NT projects this is the dominant infrastructure cost, not the planning contribution.
NT.practitionerName: Building practitioner registration with the NT Building Practitioners Board under the Building Act 1993 (NT) — categories include building contractor (residential, restricted/unrestricted), building contractor (commercial, restricted/unrestricted, mandatory for class 1b and classes 3–9 work from 15 April 2025), building certifier, certifying engineer (structural), certifying plumber/drainer (design), and owner-builder. Registration criteria (qualifications, experience, insurance) are set by Ministerial Determination (current determination gazetted 5 September 2025, Gazette No. S57). Building contractors must show and maintain net tangible assets of at least $50,000. Note that NT uses private building certifiers, who issue building permits inside declared building control areas.
quirks: Lowest warranty trigger in Australia: fidelity fund cover bites at just $12,000 of contract value (vs $20,000 NSW, $16,000 VIC, $20,000 QLD/WA), so even modest renovations are captured.

Cover is deliberately partial, not full: benefits are capped at 20% of the contract price to a maximum of $200,000 — a NT purchaser is materially less protected than in NSW/VIC, and a developer cannot point to a full-replacement warranty as a selling feature.

Cover only extends to units in complexes up to three residential storeys (excluding undercroft/basement parking levels). A four-storey-plus apartment building gets NO fidelity fund cover at all, even though the builder still needs residential registration (residential building contractor registration covers residential units to any height). This is the inverse of NSW, where taller Class 2 work attracts MORE regulation.

The fidelity fund certificate is a hard gate on the critical path: the certifier cannot issue the building permit without it, and the builder cannot lawfully demand payment from the owner without it. Because issue depends on the builder passing an accountant-verified financial capacity test (net tangible assets ≥ $50,000, actuarially set builder limits), a thinly capitalised builder can simply be refused cover and the project stalls — builder balance-sheet risk is a genuine feasibility risk in NT, not just a contractual one.

The scheme is a fidelity fund, not an insurance policy: it responds only to builder death, disappearance, insolvency or cancellation of registration by the Building Practitioners Board (plus defect rectification — 1 year non-structural, 6 years structural). There is no cover for a solvent builder who simply refuses to fix defects; the owner's remedy is contractual.

The Building Act 1993 only operates fully inside declared 'building control areas' — essentially Darwin, Palmerston, Litchfield, Alice Springs, Katherine, Tennant Creek, Nhulunbuy and specified areas. Outside a building control area no building permit is required and certifiers issue 'letters of compliance' instead of permits. Lenders, insurers and later purchasers often struggle with this, so it is a due-diligence trap on rural/remote land.

Developer contributions are the exception, not the rule. There is no territory-wide charging schedule; a contribution is payable only if a gazetted contribution plan under Part 6 of the Planning Act 1999 covers the specific land, and most NT land is not covered by any plan. Feasibility models built on interstate assumptions systematically over-state NT planning contributions — and understate NT servicing costs.

Power and Water Corporation is the sole monopoly provider of electricity, water and sewerage across the Territory, and its WASSEP headworks/extension charges are quoted project-by-project rather than published as a per-lot schedule. There is no published rate to model from — you must obtain a quote, and it can dwarf the planning contribution. WASSEP fees do not apply in remote communities.

Development consent is granted by the Development Consent Authority (a Territory body with divisions), not by the local council. Councils are a referral/servicing authority and the collector of contributions, but they do not determine the application — a fundamentally different approval politics to the council-driven systems interstate.

Wind loading: virtually all developed NT is cyclonic wind region C or D, with Darwin's post-Tracy legacy driving stringent structural, cladding, glazing and shielding requirements. Build cost per square metre and structural engineering input are materially higher than for an equivalent building in a non-cyclonic region, and standard interstate house designs generally cannot be used unmodified.

Commercial building contractor registration only commenced 15 April 2025 for class 1b and classes 3–9 work (with grandfathering), so NT's non-residential licensing regime is very new and practitioner supply in some categories is thin.

Residential building consumer protection amendments commenced 30 March 2026, changing claim timeframes (claims within 90 days of becoming aware of a defect or of a trigger event) and aligning non-completion cover with approved building permit extensions. These apply only to fidelity certificates issued on or after 30 March 2026, so projects straddling that date sit under two different claim regimes.

Much NT land is Crown leasehold or subject to native title / Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act 1976 interests, and sacred site clearance under the Northern Territory Aboriginal Sacred Sites Act 1989 (an Authority Certificate from AAPA) is a practical prerequisite for many sites — a wholly separate approval track developers elsewhere never encounter.

ACT.warrantyName: Residential building work insurance (builders warranty insurance) or a fidelity fund certificate from an approved fidelity fund scheme, required under Part 6 of the Building Act 2004 (ACT)
ACT.warrantyRegulator: ACT Construction Occupations Registrar, administered through Access Canberra (with the ACT City and Environment Directorate / planning.act.gov.au publishing the scheme rules). QBE is currently the only approved insurer and the Master Builders Fidelity Fund the only approved fidelity fund scheme.
ACT.contribMechanism: The ACT has no council-based developer contributions plan (there are no local councils and no s7.11/s7.12-style contributions). Value capture instead runs through the Lease Variation Charge (LVC) on variation of a Crown lease, now under the Planning Act 2023 (ACT) and the annual Planning (Lease Variation Charges) Determination (currently the 2026 determination; previously the Planning and Development Act 2007 and its Lease Variation Charges Determinations, and before 2011 the Change of Use Charge/betterment). LVC is either valuation-based at 75% of the value uplift (V1 - V2) x 75%, or a codified per-dwelling amount: Schedule 1 for varying a lease to specify the number of dwellings (to enable unit titling) at $49,000 per dwelling from 1 July 2026 (was $46,000 under the 2025 determination for RZ2/RZ3); Schedule 2 for increasing the permitted number of dwellings, codified by zone/locality, historically ~$40,000 to ~$300,000 per dwelling; Schedule 3 for commercial/industrial GFA. Reductions apply for RZ1 dual occupancy (RZ1 LVC partial waiver) and for social/affordable rental developments. Separately, Icon Water levies a Water and Sewerage Capital Contribution (WSCC) under the ICRC-approved WSCC Code on infill development inside designated precincts, priced per additional equivalent person ($961 per EP for 2025-26, down from $987 in 2024-25; revised code effective 1 February 2026 lowering the EP factor for small secondary dwellings from 3.5 to 2.5). Greenfield sites bought from the Suburban Land Agency generally already carry a lease permitting the dwellings, so LVC is nil and infrastructure cost is embedded in the land price / lease release conditions instead.
ACT.practitionerName: ACT Property Developer Licence under the Property Developers Act 2024 (ACT) — a distinct additional regime beyond ordinary construction occupations (builder) licensing, applying to residential projects of three or more dwellings. IMPORTANT CAVEAT FOR THE PARENT: this is a developer licensing/accountability scheme, not a NSW-DBP-style registered design practitioner and regulated design declaration regime, and its trigger is 3+ dwellings (Class 1 or Class 2), not Class 2 alone. It is genuinely a distinct additional regulated compliance cost on multi-unit residential work (licence fees, a mandatory third-party rating report, a Code of Practice, and rectification order exposure for serious defects), which is why hasClass2Regime is set true — override to false if the intended semantics are strictly design-practitioner declarations. Applications opened 1 October 2025; holding a licence becomes mandatory from 1 October 2026.
quirks: All ACT land is Crown leasehold (typically 99-year leases with a binding purpose clause), not freehold. Nearly any change in permitted use or dwelling yield requires a lease variation, and the Lease Variation Charge is the single biggest ACT-specific feasibility line item - $49,000 per dwelling codified from 1 July 2026 just to specify dwelling numbers in the lease so the site can be unit titled, or 75% of assessed value uplift where not codified.

Residential building work insurance does NOT apply to apartment buildings of more than three storeys (excluding basement carpark) - such work falls outside the definition of 'residential building work' in s 84 of the Building Act 2004. So a mid/high-rise Class 2 project carries no warranty premium at all, but purchasers also get no last-resort cover, which is a live sales and reputational issue in Canberra following well-publicised apartment defect disputes.

Where cover is required, it is capped: minimum insured amount per dwelling rose from $85,000 to $200,000 on 1 January 2025 and the claim lodgement window from 90 to 180 days. The cap is per dwelling and is widely criticised as inadequate for current build costs.

Only two providers exist: QBE (the sole approved insurer) and the Master Builders Fidelity Fund (the sole approved fidelity fund scheme, which issues a certificate rather than an insurance policy and covers 5 years, with cheaper rates for MBA members). Capacity and eligibility rather than price is often the binding constraint for a builder.

Property Developers Act 2024 (ACT): from 1 October 2026 it is mandatory to hold a property developer licence for any residential project of three or more dwellings (Class 1 or Class 2). Fees are $1,000 application, $1,000 per annual licence term, $500 per residential dwelling payable at building approval stage, and $500 to vary. Applicants must obtain a third-party capability/capacity rating report (e.g. iCIRT from Equifax, roughly $1,750 to $9,950 ex GST depending on report type and company size), comply with a Code of Practice, and are exposed to rectification orders for serious defects. Licences have already been revoked over defects. Single dwellings and dual occupancies are out of scope.

No councils and no development contributions plans - one territory-wide planning authority, one Territory Plan (2023) and one DA pathway under the Planning Act 2023. This removes council-by-council contribution variability but concentrates all discretion in one agency.

Icon Water's Water and Sewerage Capital Contribution applies only to infill inside designated precincts and is charged per additional equivalent person ($961 per EP in 2025-26). Two identical projects can differ by thousands of dollars per dwelling purely on whether the block sits inside a precinct boundary.

All-electric mandate: a regulation preventing new gas network connections commenced 8 December 2023, and buildings captured by it (all residential, plus commercial and community facility zones) must be designed and built all-electric from 1 March 2024 unless exempted. Transitional relief only for DAs lodged and BAs issued before that date. Budget for heat pumps, induction and increased electrical capacity, and expect no gas cooking as a sales feature.

Unit titling is a separate regulated step from block subdivision (Unit Titles Act 2001 and the Unit Titles (Management) Act 2011), and the Crown lease must first permit the relevant number of dwellings - hence the Schedule 1 LVC. Check ACT planning Advisory Note AN19 on block subdivision versus unit title subdivision in residential zones.
Targeted LVC relief exists and is worth structuring for: the RZ1 dual occupancy partial waiver and LVC reductions for social and affordable rental developments.

# COMPLETENESS ASSESSMENT — 8 AU jurisdictions, duty + land tax + extras

## 1. Ship / no-ship per jurisdiction

Two separate datasets are being shipped under one label. I am calling them separately, because the core rate schedules and the EXTRAS block are not remotely the same quality tier.

| Jurisdiction | Duty + land tax core | EXTRAS (warranty / contributions / practitioner) |
|---|---|---|
| **NSW** | **SHIP** — verbatim confirmed, 3-year premium-anchor reconciliation, 5 official land tax examples exact | **HOLD** — see s7.11/s7.12 provenance below |
| **VIC** | **SHIP** — 13 official duty figures exact, AOS cross-check reconciles all 15 land tax rows | **DO NOT SHIP** — premium rate inferred, gazette never read (403) |
| **QLD** | **SHIP** — verifier found zero wrong numbers; `needs_correction` is additive notes only | **DO NOT SHIP** — snippet-sourced, unresolved $36,670.70 vs $28,335.90 conflict |
| **SA** | **SHIP with a hard regime gate** (see §5) | **DO NOT SHIP** — three conflicting open-space figures for one year |
| **WA** | **SHIP** — 5 official examples exact incl. two straddling the top band | **DO NOT SHIP** — premium rate has *no source at all*, self-described estimate |
| **TAS** | **SHIP** — land tax example exact, duty chain continuous at all 6 seams | **HOLD** — correct today, but flips entirely if the 2023 Act is proclaimed |
| **ACT** | **SHIP** — 4 live-calculator runs exact, statute (DI2026-155/152) verified | **DO NOT SHIP** — LVC determinations never read (403) |
| **NT** | **DO NOT SHIP AS-IS** — one field defect will return $0 duty on real sites (§4) | **DO NOT SHIP** — premium sources conflict 2:1 |

Blunt summary: **7 of 8 core schedules are the best-verified tax data I have seen in a feasibility tool. 6 of 8 extras blocks were researched with Firecrawl returning 402 and WebFetch returning 403 — they are search-engine snippets and author estimates, not transcriptions.** Do not let the second tier ride on the first tier's credibility.

The four `needs_correction` verdicts (QLD, WA, ACT, NT) are misleading as ship signals: in all four the verifier explicitly found **no wrong rate, threshold, fixed amount or band edge**. QLD, WA and ACT are corrections to *notes and metadata*. Only NT has a defect in the data itself.

## 2. Cross-jurisdiction sanity

**Aggregate plausibility passes, and this is strong evidence.** Duty on a $3,000,000 site, computed from the shipped bands: TAS $130,185 · ACT $136,200 · WA $145,565 · NSW $146,287 · QLD $153,025 · SA $158,830 · NT $172,500 · VIC $175,000. A $130k–$175k spread with no outlier. Land tax on a $3m company-held site: ACT $24,878 · SA $25,920 · NSW $30,900 · VIC $31,650 · WA $34,330 (incl. MRIT) · TAS $39,238 · QLD $45,000 · NT $0. Coherent. No figure is implausible next to its neighbours.

**Suspiciously identical numbers — the carried-assumption check:**

- **WA and TAS duty top bands both begin at exactly $725,000.** This is the textbook signature of a researcher carrying a neighbour's figure. **Cleared, both ways.** WA's $725,000 is pinned by the official $850,000 → $34,890.50 example, which only reproduces from `from=725000, fixed=28453`. TAS's is pinned by its own continuity chain ($375,000 + $350,000 = $725,000, yielding the published $27,810). Two independent arithmetic proofs. Genuine coincidence — but document it, or the next reviewer will "fix" one of them.
- **Home warranty threshold = $20,000 in NSW, VIC, SA and WA. Four identical.** Plus **$12,000 in ACT and NT**. This is the single most likely carried assumption in the whole set. NSW $20,000 and WA $20,000 are right. **VIC $20,000 and SA $20,000 are the ones to re-verify** — Victoria's long-standing DBI threshold was $16,000 and SA's BII threshold was $12,000. Both transcribers listed the figure as confirmed; neither read the commencing regulation (VIC gazette 403'd; SA CBS 403'd). If either is a carried NSW figure it changes when the cost switches on, not its size.
- **ACT `landTaxThreshold: 0` and NT `landTaxThreshold: 0`** mean completely different things (ACT: taxed from the first dollar; NT: the tax does not exist). Identical in the data. It happens to compute correctly only because NT's `landTaxBands` is empty. Correct by luck, not by design.
- **NSW `dutyTopRate.upTo` = VIC = QLD = ... = 999999999999** across all eight. Fine as a sentinel, but it is a magic number appearing in a currency field.

**Checked and real, despite looking wrong:**
- SA's top duty band starts at **$500,000** — one-third of NSW's $1.29m and one-sixth of VIC's $2m. Real: the SA scale is unindexed and dates to circa 2010.
- ACT duty at $600,000 is **$15,720** vs VIC's $31,070 — a 2x spread. Real: the ACT has been cutting conveyance duty for years.
- TAS land tax at $3m ($39,238) exceeds NSW ($30,900) despite far lower land values. Real: 1.5% top rate entering at only $500,000.
- VIC land tax threshold **$50,000** vs NSW **$1,075,000** — a 21x spread. Real, and offset by much lower VIC marginal rates.

**Two traps where the arithmetically "correct" figure is the wrong one.** Flag these in code comments or someone will break them:
- **NSW `$1,662`** at the $103,000 band. True cumulative is $1,662.50. Revenue NSW rounded down and propagated the rounded value into $11,602, $52,237 and $194,137 — none of which reconcile off $1,662.50. "Fixing" it puts the model 50c high on every value above $103,000.
- **WA `$28,453`** at the $725,000 band. Accumulating the lower bands gives $28,452.50. The official $850,000 → $34,890.50 and $1,000,000 → $42,615.50 prove $28,453 is the operative constant. "Fixing" it is wrong by 50c forever above $725,000. WA's own transcriber described this backwards ("RevenueWA rounds up") and invited exactly that wrong fix.

## 3. False Class 2 practitioner regimes

Two non-NSW jurisdictions claim `hasClass2Regime: true`. **Both are wrong for the field's evident semantics, and both transcribers said so themselves.**

- **VIC — set to FALSE.** The transcriber's own note: "the MECHANISM is NOT the NSW one — Victoria does NOT have NSW-style registered design practitioners lodging regulated design declarations." What they actually found is the Developer Bond Scheme (2% of build cost, 4+ storeys), which (i) **does not bite until building permits issued from 1 July 2027** and is therefore not an operative cost at today's date, (ii) is **refundable capital**, so its true cost is the cost of money plus drawdown, not 2%, and (iii) triggers on storeys, not Class 2. A downstream model switching on this flag will load 2% of build cost into a 2026 feasibility for a cost that does not exist yet and is mostly recoverable.
- **ACT — set to FALSE.** The Property Developers Act 2024 licence is a developer accountability scheme, triggered at **3+ dwellings including Class 1**, not Class 2, and it is **not mandatory until 1 October 2026** — after today's 5 August 2026 date. Again self-flagged: "override to false if the intended semantics are strictly design-practitioner declarations."

QLD, SA, WA, TAS and NT are all correctly `false`. QLD, SA, WA and TAS reached that conclusion by absence-of-evidence with primary text unread (403s) — the conclusion is right, the evidence is thin. NT's is thin *and* internally unresolved: its own note says it could not determine whether Class 2 falls in the residential or the new commercial registration category, because the commercial category is described as "class 1b and classes 3 to 9" — which omits Class 2 entirely.

**Net: only NSW should carry `true`. Flip VIC and ACT.**

## 4. Worked-example arithmetic — LOUD

**Zero arithmetic failures across all eight jurisdictions.** Every official worked figure that exists reconciles to the cent off the transcribed bands: QLD $850,000 → $31,275; SA $600,000 → $26,830 plus 8 rate-chart spot checks; WA five figures including $850,000 → $34,890.50; VIC thirteen figures including $7,000,000 → $435,000; TAS ALV $400,000 → $1,287.50; ACT four live-calculator runs including $3,000,000 → $136,200; NSW's $194,137 premium anchor and four land tax examples; ACT's $1,778 × 92/365 = $448.15. NT's example even *resolved a coefficient dispute* — 0.06571441 reproduces the official $3,388, the brochure's 0.06574141 does not.

That is the single most reassuring result in this assessment and it should be stated plainly.

**But the shipped `dutyWorkedExample` field is a liability in six of eight jurisdictions, and one of those is an outright defect:**

**NT is the loud one. `dutyWorkedExample: [140000, 3388]` cannot be reproduced from NT's own shipped bands.** $140,000 falls in NT band 1, which is a quadratic the schema cannot express, and which the transcriber deliberately set to `fixed=0, rate=0`. Run the shipped example against the shipped bands and you get **$0 against an expected $3,388**. It is also the wrong *kind* of example — it is a business-property (goodwill + plant) transaction under a head of duty **abolished 9 May 2023**, and NT publishes no land conveyance example at any value. And band 1 carries `kind: "flat"`, which is affirmatively false for a quadratic, so a consumer switching on `kind` gets a silent flat 0% rather than the loud failure the transcriber intended. **$525,000 is an entirely realistic NT development site price. This returns $0 duty, silently, and it is the only field in the whole set that is internally self-contradictory.**

**NSW, VIC, WA, TAS and ACT all ship `dutyWorkedExample: [0, 0]`** while an officially published, verifier-reconciled anchor exists for every one of them (NSW $3,870,000 → $194,137; VIC $7,000,000 → $435,000 or $4,000,000 → $240,000; WA $850,000 → $34,890.50; TAS none for duty, but $400,000 → $1,287.50 for land tax; ACT $800,000 → $25,150). `[0, 0]` is worse than empty: it asserts "$0 dutiable value yields $0 duty," which **contradicts NSW's own `dutyMinimum: 20` and TAS's `dutyMinimum: 50`**, and any regression test asserting example → duty passes trivially and protects nothing. Five jurisdictions ship with the regression harness disabled.

**Only QLD and SA ship an example that both exists and reproduces from the bands.** Two of eight.

## 5. The single biggest remaining risk

**The schema cannot express *which duty regime applies*, and in four jurisdictions the correct answer for a commercial or industrial development site is a completely different number — sometimes zero.** This is the largest single-figure error in the set and it is silent.

- **SA is the worst case. Since 1 July 2018 there is NO conveyance duty at all on non-residential, non-primary-production land.** The transcribed 9-band scale applies only to residential and primary production. A commercial-zoned $3,000,000 SA site: the data says **$158,830**; the truth is **$0**. The determinant is the Valuer-General's Land Use Code plus PDI Act 2016 zoning — unknowable from purchase price. And RevenueSA publishes two *mutually inconsistent* LUC range sets (Commercial 2000-2999 vs 2000-2990; Industrial 3100-3999 vs 3100-3909) and its own calculator page omits Hotel/Motel 1810/1820/1831 from the duty-free list. The tool must ask the user; it cannot infer.
- **ACT: the commercial schedule is NIL to $2,100,000, then flat 5% of the *whole* value.** A $2,100,000 commercial site is **$0**; $2,100,001 is **$105,000**. The transcribed non-commercial schedule says ~$95,340 at $2.1m. Wrong on both sides of the cliff. ACT's own note also phrases this as "5% applied to the total transaction value **above** $2,100,000" — wording that invites an implementer to charge 5% of the excess, a 20x understatement at the threshold.
- **VIC: commercial/industrial property entered the CIPT reform from 1 July 2024** — duty once, then later dealings potentially exempt, plus an annual CIPT whose rate **no SRO current-rates page publishes** (the commonly cited 1% is unverified, and the verifier enumerated the full rates index to confirm the absence).
- **NSW premium duty (7% above $3,870,000) and QLD AFAD are residential-only**, correctly excluded from the bands but with no field to express the exclusion.

A feasibility tool that takes a purchase price and a state code and returns a duty figure will be **catastrophically wrong on a commercial SA or ACT site — up to 100% of the acquisition duty line** — while every individual number in the dataset is verbatim correct. This is a schema failure, not a research failure, and it dwarfs every rounding, boundary and band issue combined.

Close second, and the reason I split the ship call in §1: **the EXTRAS block is estimates presented in the same field shapes as verified data.** Six of eight extras were assembled with all primary retrieval blocked. If a client sees a warranty premium rate and a duty rate in adjacent columns, they will assume the same provenance. They do not have it.

Runner-up mechanical risks worth fixing before ship: **boundary conventions are inconsistent across jurisdictions with no machine-readable flag** (VIC duty needs `from < v <= upTo` while VIC land tax needs `from <= v < upTo`; TAS land tax needs `>=` at $125,000; NSW/QLD/SA are half-open) — VIC mis-prices exactly one value, $960,000, returning $52,800 instead of $52,670. And **six of eight duty schedules require a `ceil(excess/100)` rounding rule** ("or part of $100": NSW, QLD, SA, WA, TAS, ACT) while VIC does not and NT rounds *down* to the nearest 5c — with no flag in the schema for either.

## Specific numbers I would not put in front of a client

**Data defects:**
- **NT `dutyWorkedExample: [140000, 3388]`** — contradicts NT's own bands, which return $0. Wrong head of duty (abolished 9 May 2023).
- **NT band 1 `fixed: 0, rate: 0, kind: "flat"`** — silently returns $0 duty on any NT site up to and including $525,000.
- **`dutyWorkedExample: [0, 0]` in NSW, VIC, WA, TAS, ACT** — asserts $0 → $0, contradicting NSW `dutyMinimum: 20` and TAS `dutyMinimum: 50`.
- **VIC `hasClass2Regime: true`** and the 2% developer bond as a current cost — not operative until permits from 1 July 2027, and refundable capital.
- **ACT `hasClass2Regime: true`** — licence not mandatory until 1 October 2026; trigger is 3+ dwellings, not Class 2.

**Warranty premium rates — all six of these are estimates, not rates:**
- **WA `warrantyRate: 0.003`** (0.15–0.7% band) — the transcriber states plainly it is "my estimate, NOT a sourced figure," with *no* source located, plus an unconfirmed report that premiums needed to rise ~40%.
- **VIC `warrantyRate: 0.013`** — inferred from two anchors the transcriber concedes are "mutually inconsistent" (1.28% of a $500k build vs government's "less than 1 per cent"); the Premiums Order gazette (G26/2026) returned 403.
- **NT `warrantyRate: 0.007`** — the two figures found were 1.2% and ~0.6%. A 2:1 conflict split down the middle.
- **QLD `warrantyRate: 0.0056`** — interpolated from two anchors at a single $180,000 value that themselves differ 70% (new build 0.565% vs alterations 0.962%); the table above $300k was never opened.
- **ACT `warrantyRate: 0.005`** and **SA `warrantyRate: 0.0045`** — both explicitly order-of-magnitude placeholders.
- **NSW `warrantyHigh: 0.135`** — this one is *real* (icare metro H03) but applies to a narrow slice of stock and is blunted by the $340,000 per-certificate cap. Applied broadly it will kill an otherwise viable feasibility. Use 1.1–1.2%.
- **TAS `warrantyExists: false` / `warrantyRate: 0`** — correct today, but the entire finding hinges on the Residential Building (Home Warranty Insurance Amendments) Act 2023 not having been proclaimed, which was never checked against the Gazette.

**Contribution figures — every per-dwelling point estimate in the set is a synthesis:**
- **QLD `$22,000` per dwelling** — a judgement midpoint inside a $4,000–$37,000 envelope (9x range).
- **QLD `$36,670.70`** maximum adopted charge — conflicts with a separately sourced `$28,335.90`, unresolved; Planning Regulation 2017 sch 16 never opened.
- **WA `$10,000`** (range $0–$30,000) — built from two non-representative DCPs, blending land-inclusive cell arrangements with community-infrastructure DCPs, which behave nothing alike.
- **TAS `$12,000`** (range $3,000–$40,000) — the "$5,000 per lot average" underpinning it is secondary commentary.
- **SA open space: `$7,253` vs `$10,166` vs `$3,723`** — three mutually inconsistent figures for the same year, and some SA pages still describe the scheme under the *repealed* Development Act 1993.
- **SA SA Water `$5,120 + $5,120`** — confirmed for 2025-26 only; the 2026-27 schedule that actually governs approvals right now was never retrieved.
- **ACT `$49,000` per dwelling LVC and the `$40,000–$300,000` Schedule 2 range** — the Planning (Lease Variation Charges) Determination 2026 returned 403.
- **VIC greenfield per-dwelling** — requires the author's own 15–20 dwellings/net developable hectare assumption plus an assumed land value. Change the yield and the number moves a lot.
- **NSW s7.12 percentage table** — taken from a February 2021 practice note that cites **cl 25K of the repealed EP&A Regulation 2000**, not cl 209 of the 2021 Regulation. The **$20,000/$30,000 s7.11 caps** were confirmed only from an IPART-review page and an LGNSW submission arguing for their removal; the Ministerial Direction was never read.

**Practitioner costs:** VIC's upper bound bundles **$6,500–$7,000** third-party commercial courses with the **$1,039–$1,455** regulatory fee. Ship the regulatory figure only. Every `practitionerMonths` value in the set (NSW, VIC ~6, QLD 6–8 weeks, SA 6–8 weeks, ACT 3) is an estimate — no jurisdiction publishes a processing service standard.

**Minor but stated wrongly:** SA's rounding bound is given as "$5.49 duty / $2.39 land tax." The supremum is **$5.50 / $2.40** — one cent above a band floor rounds to a full $100. A bound that is not a bound.
